Raynolds]]{{NoteTag|As the land surrounding the peak has been inhabited by Indigenous peoples for time immemorial, it is assumed that it had been ascended by those people prior to 1848.}} | easiest_route = moderate snow/ice climb }} '''Citlaltépetl''' (from [[Nahuan languages|Náhuatl]] {{lang|nah|citlal(in)}} = star, and {{lang|nah|tepētl}} = mountain), otherwise known as '''Pico de Orizaba''', is an active [[volcano]] and the highest volcano in North America, as well as the highest [[mountain]] in [[Mexico]]{{cite web|url=http://utsa.edu/pub/sombrilla/pdfs/summer2003.pdf|last=Brown|first=Stephen|title=Orizaba|page=23|work=Sombrilla|publisher=University of Texas at San Antonio|year=2003|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051030031654/http://utsa.edu/pub/sombrilla/pdfs/summer2003.pdf|archive-date=October 30, 2005}} and [[Table of the highest major summits of North America|third highest peak]] in [[North America]], after [[Denali]] of the [[United States]] and [[Mount Logan]] of [[Canada]]. It rises {{convert|5,636|m}} above sea level in the eastern end of the [[Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt]], on the border between the states of [[Veracruz]] and [[Puebla]]. The volcano is currently [[dormant volcano|dormant]] but not [[extinct volcano|extinct]], with the last eruption taking place during the 19th century. It is the second most [[topographic prominence|prominent]] volcanic peak in the world after [[Mount Kilimanjaro]]. Pico de Orizaba is ranked 16th by [[topographic isolation]].{{Cite web |date=2021-10-27 |title=Pico de Orizaba |url=https://www.worldatlas.com/mountains/pico-de-orizaba.html |access-date=2025-03-20 |website=WorldAtlas |language=en-US}} ==Toponymy== Pico de Orizaba overlooks the valley and city of [[Orizaba]], from which it gets its Spanish name – literally ''"Orizaba's [[Summit|peak]]"''. During the colonial era, the volcano was also known as '''Cerro de San Andrés''' due to the nearby settlement of [[Ciudad Serdán|San Andrés Chalchicomula]] at its base.{{Cite web |last=Lara |first=Pamela Camacho |date=2021-10-01 |title=Facts about Pico de Orizaba the highest volcano in Mexico |url=https://www.poblanerias.com/2021/10/english-why-is-it-called-pico-de-orizaba/ |access-date=2025-03-20 |language=es}} Its Náhuatl name, Citlaltépetl, comes from ''[https://es.wiktionary.org/wiki/citlalli citlalli]'' (star) and [https://es.wiktionary.org/wiki/tep%C4%93tl tepētl] (mountain) and thus means "Star Mountain". This name is thought to be based on the fact that the snow-covered peak can be seen year round for hundreds of kilometers throughout the region.{{citation needed|date=December 2017}} This name is not, however, used by the [[Orizaba Nahuatl|contemporary Náhuatl speakers of the Orizaba area]], who instead call it '''''Istaktepetl''''' (o''r '''Iztactépetl'''''{{Cite web |title=Global Volcanism Program {{!}} Pico de Orizaba |url=https://volcano.si.edu/volcano.cfm?vn=341100 |access-date=2025-03-20 |website=Smithsonian Institution {{!}} Global Volcanism Program |language=en}} in the traditional orthography for [[Classical Nahuatl]]), meaning 'White Mountain'.{{Cite web |date=2019-06-01 |title=Etimologías falsas |url=https://visionlinguistica.wordpress.com/2019/06/01/etimologias-falsas/ |access-date=2025-03-20 |website=Visión lingüística |language=es}} The name Citlaltepetl is now believed to have been invented by a Spanish speaker who was likely knowledgeable in Náhuatl, but was unfamiliar with the actual name of the mountain itself.David Tuggy (15 July 2018). «[https://web.archive.org/web/20180716171427/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JHAZyl49jQE&gl=US&hl=en Aprende Náhuatl Básico: SUSTANTIVOS]». Archived from [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JHAZyl49jQE the original] on 16 July 2018. Retrieved on the 16 July 2018 A third name, '''Poyauhtecatl''', which means "the one that colours or illuminates", has also been recorded. This name was given by the [[Tlaxcaltec]]s in memory of their lost country.Map of Cuauhtinchan 2 Vol 2. Keiko Yoneda. p 239 ==Topography== The peak of Citlaltépetl rises dramatically to an elevation of {{convert|5,636|m|abbr=on}} above sea level; it has a [[topographic prominence]] of {{convert|4,922|m|abbr=on}}. Regionally dominant, Pico de Orizaba is the highest peak in Mexico and the highest volcano in North America; it is also the third highest peak in North America after [[Denali]] and [[Mount Logan]]. Orizaba is ranked [[List of peaks by prominence|7th]] in the world in [[topographic prominence]]. It is the second most prominent [[Volcanic Seven Summits|volcanic peak]] in the world after Africa's [[Mount Kilimanjaro]], and the volcano is ranked 16th in the world for [[topographic isolation]]. About {{convert|110|km|abbr=on}} to the west of the port of [[Veracruz (city)|Veracruz]], its peak is visible to ships approaching the port in the [[Gulf of Mexico]], and at dawn rays of sunlight strike the Pico while Veracruz still lies in shadow. The topography of Pico de Orizaba is [[Asymmetry|asymmetrical]] from the center of the crater; the eastern face is the steepest side of the volcano and the northwestern face the most gradual side. The gradual slopes of the northwestern face of the volcano allow for the presence of large glaciers and provide the most traveled route for hikers traveling to the summit. ==Glaciers== [[File:Citlaltépetl Glaciers.svg|thumb|right|The main peaks and glaciers of Pico de Orizaba]] Pico de Orizaba is one of only three volcanoes in México that continue to support glaciers and is home to the largest glacier in Mexico, [[Gran Glaciar Norte]]. Orizaba has nine known glaciers: Gran Glaciar Norte, Lengua del Chichimeco, Jamapa, Toro, Glaciar de la Barba, Noroccidental, Occidental, Suroccidental, and Oriental. The [[Snow line|equilibrium line altitude]] (ELA) is not known for Orizaba. Snow on the south and southeast sides of the volcano melts quickly because of solar radiation, but lower temperatures on the northwest and north sides allow for glaciers. The insolation angle and wind redeposition on the northwest and north sides allow for constant accumulation of snow providing a source for the [[Glacier#Types|outlet glaciers]]. On the north side of Orizaba, the Gran Glaciar Norte fills the elongated highland basin and is the source for seven outlet glaciers. The main glacier extends {{convert|3.5|km|abbr=on}} north of the crater rim, has a surface area of about {{convert|9.08|km2|abbr=on}} descending from {{convert|5650|m|abbr=on}} to about {{convert|5000|m|abbr=on}}. It has a slightly irregular and stepped profile that is caused in part by the configuration of the bedrock. Most [[crevasses]] show an ice thickness of approximately {{convert|50|m|abbr=on}}.{{cite web |last=White |first=Sidney E. |title=Glaciers of North America: Glaciers of México |publisher=[[U.S. Geological Survey]] |date=March 7, 2002 |url=https://pubs.usgs.gov/pp/p1386j/mexico/mexico-lores.pdf |access-date=2011-02-20 }} [[File:Pico de Orizaba 1 Zoom.jpg|thumb|left|Pico de Orizaba looking south from atop [[Cofre de Perote]]]] Below the {{convert|5,000|m|ft|abbr=on}} in elevation on the north side of the volcano, the outlet glaciers Lengua del Chichimeco and Jamapa extend north and northwest another {{convert|1.5|km|mi|abbr=on}} and {{convert|2|km|mi|abbr=on}}, respectively. The terminal lobe of Lengua del Chichimeco at {{convert|4,740|m|ft|abbr=on}}, having a gradient of only {{convert|140|m/km|abbr=on}}, is a low, broad ice fan that has a convex-upward profile, a front typical of almost all Mexican glaciers. The most distinct glacier is Glaciar de Jamapa, which leaves Gran Glaciar Norte at about {{convert|4,975|m|ft|abbr=on}} and, after {{convert|2|km|mi|abbr=on}} with a gradient of {{convert|145|m/km|abbr=on}}, divides into two small tongues that end at {{convert|4,650|m|ft|abbr=on}} and {{convert|4,640|m|ft|abbr=on}}. Both tongues terminate in broad convex-upward ice fans thinning along their edges. The retreat of these tongues prior to 1994 produced much erosion downstream and buried their edges by ablation rock debris. The west side of Gran Glaciar Norte generates five outlet glaciers. From north to south, the first two, Glaciar del Toro and Glaciar de la Barba, are hanging cliff or icefall glaciers, reaching the tops of giant lava steps at {{convert|4,930|m|ft|abbr=on}} and {{convert|5,090|m|ft|abbr=on}}, respectively. They then descend {{convert|200|to|300|m|ft|abbr=on}} farther down into the heads of stream valleys as huge ice blocks but are not regenerated there. About {{convert|1|km|mi|abbr=on}}, Glaciar Noroccidental, a small outlet glacier {{convert|300|m|ft|abbr=on}} long, drains away from the side of Gran Glaciar Norte at about {{convert|5,100|m|ft|abbr=on}} and draws down the ice surface a few tens of meters over a distance of {{convert|500|m|ft|abbr=on}}, descending to {{convert|4,920|m|ft|abbr=on}} with a gradient of {{convert|255|m/km|abbr=on}}. Another {{convert|1|km|mi|abbr=on}} still farther south, Glaciar Occidental breaks away from Gran Glaciar Norte west of the summit crater at about {{convert|5,175|m|ft|abbr=on}} as a steep, {{convert|1|km|mi|abbr=on}} long glacier having a gradient of {{convert|270|m/km|abbr=on}} that ends at {{convert|4,930|m|ft|abbr=on}}. From the southwest corner of the mountain, another outlet glacier, Glaciar Suroccidental, {{convert|1.6|km|mi|abbr=on}} long, flows from Gran Glaciar Norte at {{convert|5,250|m|ft|abbr=on}} with a gradient of {{convert|200|m/km|abbr=on}}, which also ends at {{convert|4,930|m|ft|abbr=on}} in a long smooth surface. East of the summit cone, a separate steep niche glacier, Glaciar Oriental, {{convert|1.2|km|abbr=on}} long and having a gradient of {{convert|440|m/km|abbr=on}}, flows down the mountainside from about {{convert|5,600|to|5,070|m|ft|abbr=on}}; it contains many crevasses and seracs and is the most difficult glacier to climb. Glacier Oriental had a surface area of about {{convert|420,000|m2|sqft|abbr=on}} in 1958, which makes the total area of glaciers and firn field on Citlaltépetl about {{convert|9.5|km2|sqmi|abbr=on}}. No earlier historical record of glacier tongue activity (advance or recession) is known for Citlaltépetl's glaciers. Although the Gran Glaciar Norte ice cap is covered with snow, it is possible to see the seven outlet glaciers on the irregular west margin of the ice cap, especially Glaciar de Jamapa and Glaciar Occidental. ==Climate== {{unreferenced section|date=November 2017}} {{multiple image |align=right |direction=verical |width= |image1=Citlaltepetll.jpg |caption1=Southeast of Citlaltépetl |image2=Citlalepetl2.JPG |caption2=Northwest of Citlaltépetl }} The climate of Pico de Orizaba, like the [[Sierra Madre Oriental]], varies greatly due to the change of elevation and [[prevailing winds]]. Due to the latitude and the extreme rugged terrain the volcano experiences many [[microclimate]]s. Vegetation varies from tropical at the lower elevations on the eastern face to alpine forests in the higher elevations. Large amounts of precipitation fall on the eastern face of the volcano due to [[adiabatic cooling]] and condensation from the [[trade winds]] that bring moisture off the Gulf of Mexico. The eastern face is frequently covered by fog and low cloud cover. The climate of the eastern face varies from tropical [[Tropical rainforest climate|(Af)]] at the lower elevations to subtropical highland [[Oceanic climate#Subtropical highland variety (Cfb, Cwb)|(Cfb)]] at the higher elevations, with mild variation in temperatures and an average annual rainfall of {{convert|1,600|mm|in|abbr=on}}. Subtropical climates are found between {{convert|2,200|and|3,200|m|ft|abbr=on}} above sea level with a regular rainfall all year long. Autumn and winter come with frequent freezes and light snow, but the snow on the south and southeast sides melt quickly due to solar radiation. The northern face is dominated by subtropical highland [[Oceanic climate#Subtropical highland variety (Cfb, Cwb)|(Cwb)]]. The southern face mostly experiences a humid subtropical climate, [[Humid subtropical climate|(Cwa)]] with the highest annual temperatures in the month of April. Due to [[katabatic wind]]s the western side is dominated by steppe [[Semi-arid climate|(BSk)]] creating a rain shadow below {{convert|2600|m|ft|abbr=on}} above sea level. Although there are some areas on the western side that experience [[Humid subtropical climate|(Cfa)]] most of the area is semi-dry with temperate to warm temperatures and an annual precipitation average of {{convert|550|mm|in|abbr=on}}. Vegetation here is grass and shrubs with few alpine species. Between {{convert|3,200|and|4,300|m|ft|abbr=on}}, where temperatures usually are between {{convert|2|and|5|C|F}}, a cold-summer version of the subtropical highland climate [[Oceanic climate#Subpolar oceanic and cold subtropical highland varieties (Cfc, Cwc)|(Cfc)]] predominates. Over {{convert|4,300|m|ft|abbr=on}} with an annual average low of {{convert|-2|C|F}}, [[alpine tundra]] [[Polar climate|(ET)]] prevails to the summit; heavy snowfalls and blizzards are common throughout the year. Snow on the south and southeast melts due to solar radiation, but continually remains on the north and northwestern faces. Extreme cold dominates a surface area of approximately {{convert|31|km2|sqmi|abbr=on}}. ==Geology== [[File:Pico de Orizaba caldera.jpg|thumb|[[Caldera]]]] Pico de Orizaba evolved in three stages, the most recent initiated about 16,000 years ago during the late [[Pleistocene]] and [[Holocene]]. Citlaltépetl consists of three superimposed stratovolcanoes and dome intrusions: Torrecillas (650–250 [[Year#Symbol|ka]]), Espolón de Oro (210– 16 ka), and Citlaltépetl (16 ka to present). The volcano was formed by thick [[Andesite|andesitic]] and [[Dacite|dacitic]] lavas that followed repetitive explosive eruptions and [[Effusive eruption|lava effusions]] that created the iconic cone structure. The volcano is currently [[dormant volcano|dormant]] but not [[extinct volcano|extinct]]. The latest eruption of the volcano occurred in 1846 with a magnitude of [[VEI]] 2. Previous eruptions occurred in: 1687, 1613, 1589–1569, 1566, 1555–1545,1539–1533, 1351, 1260, 1187, 1175, 1157, 220 AD, 140 AD, 90 AD, 40 AD, ~780 BC, ~1500 BC, ~2110 BC, ~2300 BC, ~2500 BC, ~2780 BC, ~4690 BC, ~6220 BC, ~6710 BC, ~7030 BC, and ~7530 BC.{{cite web |url=http://www.volcano.si.edu/world/volcano.cfm?vnum=1401-10=&volpage=erupt |last1=Simkin |first1=T. |last2=Siebert |first2=L. |title=Pico de Orizaba |work=[[Global Volcanism Program]] |publisher=The [[Smithsonian Institution]] |year=2002 |access-date=2011-02-20 |archive-date=2022-12-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221205172555/https://volcano.si.edu/world/volcano.cfm?vnum=1401-10=&volpage=erupt |url-status=dead }} The most violent eruption in the volcano's history is thought to have occurred around 6710 BC, reaching a magnitude of [[VEI]] 5, characterized by [[lava dome]] extrusion and [[pyroclastic flow]]. The volcano's crater is elliptical with a [[ellipse|transverse diameter]] measuring {{convert|478|m|ft|abbr=on}} and a [[ellipse|conjugate diameter]] measuring {{convert|410|m|ft|abbr=on}}. The crater has an estimated {{convert|154,830|m2|sqft|abbr=on}} with a maximum depth of {{convert|300|m|ft|abbr=on}}. Pico de Orizaba is constantly covered by an [[Glacier#Types|ice cap]] consisting of several glaciers. An outlet glacier, known as Jamapa Glacier, is located on the north-eastern side of the peak; it has been a powerful force in shaping the volcano. The Jamapa Glacier is responsible for a significant portion of the [[Geomorphology|geomorphologic]] evolution of the region surrounding the volcano.{{cite news |last1=Palacios |first1=D. |last2=Vázquez-Selem |first2=L. |title=The Geomorphic Effects of the Retreat of Jamapa Glacier, Pico de Orizaba Volcano |publisher=[[Scandinavian University Press]] |year=1996 |jstor=521132 |volume=78 |pages=19–34}} ==Geography== {{Unreferenced section|date=March 2025}}{{multiple image |align=right |direction=vertical |width= |image1=15-07-14-Landschaft-zwischen-Mexico-und-Golfküste-RalfR-WMA 0456.jpg |caption1=Aerial view |image2=Pico de Orizaba, Mexico.JPG |caption2=Shadows accentuate several features of Pico de Orizaba in this astronaut's photograph }} Pico de Orizaba is located at 19°1′48″N 97°16′12″W, about {{convert|110|km|mi}} west of the Gulf of Mexico and {{convert|200|km|mi}} east of [[Mexico City]], on the border between the states of Veracruz and Puebla. The volcano is approximately {{convert|480|km|mi}} south of the [[Tropic of Cancer]]. Orizaba anchors the south-eastern end of the [[Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt]], a volcanic chain that runs from west to east across Central Mexico. A companion peak lying about six km to the southwest of Pico de Orizaba is the [[Sierra Negra]], at {{convert|4640|m|ft|0}}. This subsidiary peak is significantly lower than its massive neighbour, but the road to the observatory on its summit is the highest road in North America. Pico de Orizaba, as part of the [[Sierra Madre Oriental]], forms a barrier between the coastal plains of the Gulf of Mexico and the [[Mexican Plateau]]. The volcano blocks the moisture from the Gulf of Mexico from saturating central Mexico and influences the climates of both areas. Both the state of Veracruz and Puebla depend on Pico de Orizaba for supplying fresh water. The largest river originating on the volcano is the [[Jamapa River]]. ==History== {{multiple image |align=right |direction=vertical |width= |image1=Church and volcano by mexikids.jpg |caption1=Hacienda de las Flores near Citlaltépetl |image2=Pico de Orizaba glacier ascent.jpg |caption2=Climber ascending the Jamapa Glacier }} Pico de Orizaba was important in pre-Hispanic cultures, such as those of the Nahuatl-speaking [[Aztec|Mexica]] and the [[Totonac]]s. The volcano is part of many native mythologies, defining Nahua folklore, [[cosmology]], and [[eschatology]].Hlúšek, Radoslav. “Mountains in the Worldview of the Nahuas of Central Mexico.” ''Český Lid'', vol. 110, no. 4, 2023, pp. 451–77. ''JSTOR'', https://www.jstor.org/stable/27278373. Accessed 20 Mar. 2025. During the [[Spanish Conquest]] of Mexico, [[Hernán Cortés]] passed through the foothills of Pico de Orizaba; the volcano and the surrounding mountains made his journey to [[Tenochtitlan]] more difficult and delayed him for many days. During the 1600s, the Spanish Crown financed several roads to be built that would circumvent Citlaltépetl. One of the roads was routed south of the volcano through the cities of Orizaba and Fortín de las Flores, which became the main trade route between Mexico City and Veracruz on the Gulf Coast. A short road was later built by [[Jesuits]] to establish settlements at the base of Pico de Orizaba. The Spanish used the volcano as a landmark to guide themselves to the port of Veracruz. Many battles were fought near this volcano throughout Mexico's struggle for independence. In 1839, [[Henri Guillaume Galeotti|Henri Galeotti]] was the first European to explore the volcano, but did not hike to the summit. During the American occupation of Mexico in 1848, two American soldiers, F. Maynard and [[William F. Raynolds]], were the first known hikers to reach the summit of Pico de Orizaba.{{Cite book |last1=Ortenburger |first1=Leigh N. |last2=Jackson |first2=Reynold G. |title=A climber's guide to the Teton Range |publisher=[[Mountaineers Books]] |date=November 1996 |page=374 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Z-Y1tLw_YWgC&q=Reynolds+peak+in+the+teton+range+named+for&pg=PA374 |isbn=0-89886-480-1}} In 1851, the French explorer Alejandro Doignon also reached the summit and found the flagpole left behind by the Americans in 1848. During the mid-19th century Citlaltépetl was explored by many scientists, including the [[Germany|German]] botanist Hugo Fink, who was the first to record the numerous species of flora found on the volcano. In 1873, [[Martin Tritschler]] raised the Mexican flag at the summit.{{citation needed|date=January 2022}} ==Pico de Orizaba National Park== On December 16, 1936, President [[Lázaro Cárdenas]], in an effort to protect the natural beauty of Pico de Orizaba, created a national park with an area of {{convert|19750|ha|acre}} that included the volcano with the surrounding area and the settlements of Tlachichuca, Ciudad Serdán, La Perla, Mariano Escobedo, and Calcahualco. The federal decree became federal law on January 4, 1937. == Climbing and recreation == {{Unreferenced section|date=March 2025}}[[File:Orizaba 18,500 feet.JPG|thumb|left|View of the standard route from the Stone Hut (Piedra Grande), shown in the bottom left of this photo - November 2007]] [[File:Pico de Orizaba traverse of crater rim.jpg|thumb|Traverse of steep slope above Glacier Este during circumnavigation of crater rim. November 2008]] Pico de Orizaba attracts a large number of international climbers every year. There are multiple routes for approaching and climbing the volcano, and many people attempt it. Most people climb the mountain during the period from October to March when the weather is favorable;{{citation needed|date=April 2017}} temperatures do not vary much month to month due to being in the tropics and April through September are rainy months in the region. The most frequented route begins from the base camp Piedra Grande Hut ("refugio") via the Jamapa Glacier, located at an elevation of {{convert|4,270|m|ft|abbr=on}} above sea level. Another option as a starting point is high camp located at the base of the glacier about {{convert|4,900|m|ft|abbr=on}} above sea level. For a more technical challenge for the experienced climber, there is a technical ice climb called the Serpents Head, which involves 10 pitches of grade 3 ice. Additionally, the southern side offers another challenging option; although the trail is shorter, it is also steeper and more difficult. No glaciers are found on the southern side. The final ascent to the summit is via a normally straightforward and crevasse-free glacier route. The caldera can be circumnavigated with relative ease, although at one point this requires a short, exposed traverse of steep rock and ice above the Glacier Este. ==See also== *[[List of mountain peaks of North America]] **[[List of mountain peaks of Mexico]] ***[[List of volcanoes in Mexico]] ***[[List of Ultras of Mexico]] *[[List of elevation extremes by country]] *[[Orizaba]] *[[Volcanic Seven Summits]] {{clear}} == Notes == ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Further reading== * {{cite gvp| 1=341100 | 2=Pico de Orizaba}} * {{cite book | last = Yarza de la Torre | first = Esperanza | title = Volcanes de México | publisher = Aguilar | year = 1971 | pages= 237 pp |ref=none}} (in Spanish) * {{cite book | last = Secor | first = R. J. | title = Mexico's Volcanoes: A Climbing Guide | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=XEqrPcMJ8vYC&q=secor%20mexico's%20volcanoes&pg=PA4 | edition = 3rd | publisher = [[Mountaineers Books]] | year = 2001 | pages= 160 pp | isbn = 0-89886-798-3 |ref=none}} ==External links== {{commons and category}} * [http://www.summitorizaba.com/equipment Equipment List to climb Pico de Orizaba] * [http://www.summitpost.org/mountain/rock/150192/pico-de-orizaba.html Pico de Orizaba on Summitpost.com] * {{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20140110163421/http://horalka.org/volcanes-de-mexico/climb/?pico-de-orizaba-citlaltepetl Pico de Orizaba - ascent route description]}} {{Navboxes|list= {{Mexico highest}} {{Puebla}}{{Veracruz}} {{NA highest}}{{NA prominent}}{{NA isolated}} {{Volcanic Seven Summits}} {{Seven Third Summits}} }} {{Portal bar|North America|Mexico|Mountains|Volcanoes| border =no}} {{Authority control}}{{Highest points of North America}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Orizaba}} [[Category:Mountains of Mexico|Pico de Orizaba]] [[Category:Landforms of Puebla|Pico de Orizaba]] [[Category:Volcanoes of Veracruz|Pico de Orizaba]] [[Category:Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt|Pico de Orizaba]] [[Category:Stratovolcanoes of Mexico]] [[Category:Seven Third Summits]] [[Category:Volcanic Seven Summits]] [[Category:Five-thousanders of North America|Pico de Orizaba]] [[Category:Highest points of countries|Pico de Orizaba]] [[Category:Religious places of the Indigenous peoples of North America]] [[Category:Sacred mountains of Mexico]] [[Category:VEI-5 volcanoes]] [[Category:National parks of Mexico]] [[Category:Protected areas of Veracruz]] [[Category:Protected areas of Puebla]] [[Category:Pleistocene stratovolcanoes]] [[Category:Holocene stratovolcanoes]]

With an elevation of 5,109 m (16,763 ft), it is the highest mountain of both the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]] and [[Uganda]], and the [[List of highest mountain peaks of Africa|fourth-highest]] in [[Africa]]{{efn|Although Mount Stanley is the third-tallest independent mountain, [[Kilimanjaro]]'s second tallest volcanic peak, Mawenzi, has sufficient promience (850 meters) to be considered an independent peak. Both [[Reinhold Messner|Messner]] and [[Richard Bass|Bass]] list Mawenzi in the [[Seven Third Summits]]}}. The peak and several other surrounding peaks are high enough to support [[glacier]]s. Mount Stanley is named for the explorer, journalist, and colonist [[Sir Henry Morton Stanley]]. It is part of the [[Rwenzori Mountains National Park]], a [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]].{{cite web|url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/684|title=Rwenzori Mountains National Park|publisher=UNESCO World Heritage Centre|access-date=11 February 2024}} == Peaks == Mt. It is located in the central part of the republic, in Aragatsotn Region, where it is isolated from the rest of the country's mountain ranges.}} However, it is considered part and the highest point of the larger [[Lesser Caucasus]] mountain range.{{cite web|title=Mount Aragats|url=http://www.britannica.com/place/Mount-Aragats|website=[[Encyclopædia Britannica]]|quote=The highest point in both Armenia and the Lesser Caucasus range...}}{{cite book|title=Encyclopedia Americana: Cathedrals to Civil War|url=https://archive.org/details/encyclopediaamer03scho|url-access=registration|date=2005|publisher=Scholastic Library Publishing|isbn=9780717201389|page=[https://archive.org/details/encyclopediaamer03scho/page/86 86]|quote=The highest point within the Armenian part of the Lesser Caucasus is Mt. Aragats...}} It has four summits, which are named according to their relative geographic position: *Northern—{{convert|4090|m|ft|abbr=on}} *Western—{{convert|3995|m|ft|abbr=on}} *Eastern—{{convert|3908|m|ft|abbr=on}} *Southern—{{convert|3888|m|ft|abbr=on}} Mount Aragats has a [[topographic prominence]] of 2,143 meters, [[List of Ultras of West Asia|more than some higher mountains]], such as [[Dykh-Tau]] (5,205 m high) in the Russian part of Great Caucasus Range. Situated {{convert|40|km|mi}} northwest of the Armenian capital [[Yerevan]], Aragats is a large volcano with numerous [[fissure vents]] and [[adventive cones]]. Numerous large lava flows descend from the volcano and are constrained in age between the middle Pleistocene and 3,000 BCE. The summit crater is cut by a {{convert|13|km|mi}} long line of cones which generated possibly Holocene-age [[lahar]]s and lava flow. The volcanic system covers an area of 5,000 km2 and is one of the largest in the region. More recent activity in flank centers occurred in Tirinkatar (0.48-0.61 Ma), Kakavasar, (0.52-0.54 Ma), and Ashtarak (0.58 Ma), as well as Jrbazhan in the summit area (0.52 Ma). The magmas feeding Aragats are unusually hot for arc-derived magmas, resulting in long and voluminous lava flows.{{cite journal|author1=Meliksetian, Khachatur|author2=Savov, Ivan|author3=Connor, Charles|author4=Halama, Ralf|author5=Jrbashyan, Ruben|author6=Navasardyan, Gevorg|author7=Ghukasyan, Yura|author8=Gevorgyan, Hripsime|author9=Manucharyan, Davit|author10=Ishizuka, Osamu|author11=Quidelleur, Xavier|year=2014|title=Aragats stratovolcano in Armenia - volcano-stratigraphy and petrology|journal=[[Geophysical Research Abstracts]]|volume=16|page=567|bibcode=2014EGUGA..16..567M|author12=Germa, Aurélie}} ===Glaciation=== Shortly after World War II, observations noted the presence of [[firn]] fields and snowfields on the sides of the crater cirque as well as moraines and glaciers inside the crater. An analysis in 1896 indicated a surface area of 5.5-5.8 km2, but it rapidly retreated afterward. The glaciation has been retreating on account of insufficient snowfall and increasing temperatures. Glacial meltwater dominates the upper part of the rivers descending from Aragats but its importance decreases farther down the valleys.{{cite journal|last1=Davoyan|first1=M.O.|year=1971|title=Area of modern glaciation on Mt. Aragats and the diminution of firn basins|journal=International Geology Review|volume=13|issue=4|pages=530–533|bibcode=1971IGRv...13..530D|doi=10.1080/00206817109475464|issn=0020-6814}} Traces of prehistorical glaciation also exist including thick moraines in the summit area at an altitude of 2,600–3,000 m.{{cite journal|last1=Maisuradze|first1=G.M.|year=1989|title=Anthropogene of the ===Geological=== The volcano was constructed in four different phases. The first phase (possibly 2.5 Ma) occurred in the main crater and subsidiary vents and was [[basaltic andesite]] in composition. It crops out in deep gorges. The second phase (0.97–0.89 Ma, by [[K–Ar dating|K–Ar]]) involved the main vent, and subsidiary structures and was [[basaltic]] and [[andesitic]] in composition with ignimbrites and pyroclastic, with tuffs and lava flows emanating from satellite centers. It was the most voluminous and included the Shamiram and Yeghvard subsidiary centres. The third phase (0.74–0.68 Ma) while similar to the second was more restricted in regional extent to the [[Mantash]] River basin. The fourth stage (0.56–0.45 Ma) involved [[mafic]] lava flows from parasitic vents in the southern parts of the volcano.{{cite journal |last1=Chernyshev |first1=I.V. |last2=Lebedev |first2=V. A. |last3=Arakelyants |first3=M. M. |last4=Jrbashyan |first4=R. T. |last5=Gukasyan |first5=Yu. G. |date=May 2002 |title=Quaternary geochronology of the Aragats volcanic center, Armenia: Evidence from K-Ar dating |journal=Doklady Earth Sciences |volume=384 |issue=4 |pages=393–398}} ===Cultural=== Numerous engravings have been made around the volcano, including rock paintings portraying animals and human-like figures in the [[Kasagh River]] valley possibly dating to the early Holocene, and in [[Aghavnatun]] on the southern side of the volcano including petroglyphs showing animals that were possibly created in the 4th to 1st millennia BCE.{{cite web|url=https://www.academia.edu/2111647|title=The Rock Art of the Mt. Aragats System|publisher=[[:it:Centro camuno di studi preistorici|Centro camuno di studi preistorici]]|date=24 May 2007|first=Anna|last=Khechoyan}} According to an ancient Armenian legend, Aragats and [[Mount Ararat]] were loving sisters who parted after a quarrel and separated permanently. Another legend tells that [[Gregory the Illuminator]], who converted Armenia to Christianity in the early 4th century, "used to pray on the peak of the mountain. At nighttime an icon lamp shone to give light to him, the lamp hanging from heaven using no rope. Some say that the icon lamp is still there, but only the worthy ones can see it." [[File:Aragats from the Plain of Alexandropol.png|thumb|Aragats from the [[Shirak Plain]], probably in 1901]] In 1935, on the 15th anniversary of [[Red Army invasion of Armenia|Armenia's Sovietization]], around one thousand people climbed the summit of Aragats from five directions.{{cite book |last1=Sekoyan |first1=V. |title=[[Armenian Soviet Encyclopedia]] Volume 13 |date=1987 |location=Yerevan |page=[https://hy.wikisource.org/wiki/%D4%B7%D5%BB:%D5%80%D5%A1%D5%B5%D5%AF%D5%A1%D5%AF%D5%A1%D5%B6_%D5%8D%D5%B8%D5%BE%D5%A5%D5%BF%D5%A1%D5%AF%D5%A1%D5%B6_%D5%80%D5%A1%D5%B6%D6%80%D5%A1%D5%A3%D5%AB%D5%BF%D5%A1%D6%80%D5%A1%D5%B6_(Soviet_Armenian_Encyclopedia)_13.djvu/324 324] |language=hy |chapter=Տուրիզմ [Tourism] |quote=1935-ին, Հայաստանում սովետական կարգերի հաստատման 15-ամյակի կապակցությամբ, ավելի քան 1000 մարդ 5 տարբեր կետից բարձրացել է Արագածի գագաթը։}} On May 28, 2005—the anniversary of the establishment of the [[First Republic of Armenia]]—around 250,000 people participated in a Dance of Unity ({{langx|hy|Միասնության շուրջպար}}) around Mount Aragats in a mass display of national unity. The quarter million participants, among them then-President [[Robert Kocharyan]] and Defense Minister [[Serzh Sargsyan]], formed a {{convert|163|km|mi|adj=on}} ring around the mountain after a blessing from Catholicos [[Karekin II]].{{cite news |last1=Stepanian |first1=Ruzanna |title=Thousands Dance To Mark Armenia's Independence Holiday |url=https://www.azatutyun.am/a/1577120.html |work=azatutyun.am |agency=[[RFE/RL]] |date=30 May 2005}}{{cite news|title=Armenian people united around Aragats mountain|url=http://www.panarmenian.net/eng/politics/news/13521/|access-date=20 June 2013|agency=[[PanARMENIAN.Net]]|date=28 May 2005}}{{cite news|title=Միասնության շուրջպարը գրկեց Արագած լեռը|url=https://armenpress.am/arm/news/418093/miasnutyan-shurjpary-grkec-aragats-lery.html|agency=[[Armenpress]]|date=28 May 2005|language=hy}} The organizers hoped the event would be included in the ''[[Guinness World Records]]''.{{cite news|last1=Vardanian|first1=Gegham|title=Armenia's Big Dance|url=https://iwpr.net/global-voices/armenias-big-dance|publisher=[[Institute for War and Peace Reporting]]|date=2 June 2005}} Prior to the dance, some 110,000 trees were planted on the slopes of Aragats.{{cite web|title=Մի ֆոտոյի պատմություն. միասնության շուրջպար |url=http://www.1tv.am/hy/news/2015/05/28/%D5%87%D5%B8%D6%82%D6%80%D5%BB%D5%BA%D5%A1%D6%80/16568 |website=1tv.am |publisher=[[Armenia 1|Public Television of Armenia]] |language=hy |date=28 May 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160429122013/http://www.1tv.am/hy/news/2015/05/28/%D5%87%D5%B8%D6%82%D6%80%D5%BB%D5%BA%D5%A1%D6%80/16568 |archive-date=April 29, 2016 }} ==Nearby settlements== The following settlements are located on the slopes or foot of Aragats: [[Ashtarak]],{{cite book|last1=Kaeter|first1=Margaret|title=The Caucasian Republics|date=2004|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=9780816052684|page=[https://archive.org/details/caucasianrepubli00kaet/page/68 68]|quote=In between Gyumri and Yerevan lies Mount Aragats, the highest mountain currently in Armenia, at about 14,000 feet. Ashtarak, the closest town of any size, has 20,000 people...|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/caucasianrepubli00kaet/page/68}} [[Artik]], [[Aparan]], [[Talin, Armenia|Talin]], [[Oshakan]], [[Byurakan]]. ==Main sights== ===Historic and cultural sites=== [[File:Arshakunyats Mausoleum 02.jpg|[[Arshakid Mausoleum]].|thumb]] [[File:Amberd fortress and church 2009.jpg|[[Amberd]] and [[Vahramashen Church]].|thumb]] [[File:Tegher Monastery.jpg|[[Tegher Monastery]].|thumb]] [[File:Հայոց այբուբենի հուշարձան, Արտաշավան.JPG|Alphabet park.|thumb]] Aragats has historically played a significant role in Armenian history and culture. Numerous historical and modern monuments are located on its slopes, some of which are listed below. The 4th-century [[Arshakid Mausoleum|mausoleum]] of the [[Arsacid dynasty of Armenia|Arsacid (Arshakuni) dynasty]] is located in the village of [[Aghtsk]], on the slopes of Aragats. The early medieval fortress of [[Amberd]] and the nearby 11th-century [[Vahramashen Church]] are located on the slopes of Aragats, at an altitude of {{convert|2300|m|ft|abbr=on}}.{{cite book|last=Ghafadaryan|first=K.|author-link=Karo Ghafadaryan|title=[[Soviet Armenian Encyclopedia]] Volume I|contribution=Ամբերդ (Amberd)|date=1974|page=[https://hy.wikisource.org/wiki/%D4%B7%D5%BB:%D5%80%D5%A1%D5%B5%D5%AF%D5%A1%D5%AF%D5%A1%D5%B6_%D5%8D%D5%B8%D5%BE%D5%A5%D5%BF%D5%A1%D5%AF%D5%A1%D5%B6_%D5%80%D5%A1%D5%B6%D6%80%D5%A1%D5%A3%D5%AB%D5%BF%D5%A1%D6%80%D5%A1%D5%B6_(Soviet_Armenian_Encyclopedia)_1.djvu/278 278–280]|language=hy}} One source calls Amberd the "biggest and the best preserved fortress" in modern-day Armenia.{{cite web|title=Ashtarak-Oshakan-Amberd fortress–Letter Park|url=http://www.wonderlandarmenia.com/index.php/fa/tours/daily-tours/49-7-ashtarak-oshakan-amberd-fortress-letter-park|website=wonderlandarmenia.com|date=2014}}{{dead link|date=February 2024|bot=medic}} The Alphabet Park ({{Transliteration|hy|Tar’eri purak}}) is located near the village of [[Artashavan]]. It was founded in 2005 on the 1600th anniversary of the invention of the [[Armenian alphabet]]. It features sculptures of the 39 letters of the [[Armenian alphabet]] and statues of notable Armenians, such as [[Mesrop Mashtots]] (the inventor of the alphabet), Armenia's national poet [[Hovhannes Tumanyan]], [[Khachatur Abovian]] (father of modern Eastern Armenian literature), and others.{{cite web|title=Հայոց այբուբենի հուշարձան|url=http://www.hyurservice.com/arm/sights/armenian_alphabet_monument_arm.html|website=hyurservice.com|publisher=Hyur Service|language=hy}} In 2012, a {{convert|33|m|ft|adj=on}} high cross, composed of 1711 large and small iron crosses, symbolizing the number of years since Armenia's conversion to Christianity in 301, was installed on a hill near the park. A cross is added on an annual basis.{{cite news|last1=Mkrtchyan|first1=Anush|title=Տառերի պուրակում տեղի ունեցավ 33 մետրանոց Սուրբ խաչի բացումը|url=https://www.azatutyun.am/content/article/24745783.html|work=azatutyun.am|agency=[[Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty]]|date=20 October 2012|language=hy}} ===Scientific institutions=== [[File:Jezero Kari.jpg|[[Lake Kari]] and the [[Aragats Cosmic Ray Research Station]] (in the background).|thumb]] The [[Aragats Cosmic Ray Research Station]] is a [[cosmic-ray observatory]] near [[Lake Kari]], at around {{convert|3200|m|ft|abbr=on}} above sea level. It was founded in 1943 by the brothers [[Artem Alikhanian]] and [[Abram Alikhanov]]. The Nor-Amberd station, built in 1960, is located at {{convert|2000|m|ft|abbr=on}}.{{cite web |title=Research Stations |url=http://crd.yerphi.am/Research_Stations |website=crd.yerphi.am |publisher=[[Yerevan Physics Institute]]}} The [[Byurakan Observatory]], established in 1946 by [[Victor Ambartsumian]], is located on the southern slopes of Aragats, near the village of [[Byurakan]], at an altitude of {{convert|1405|m|ft|abbr=on}}.{{cite web|title=History of the Byurakan Astrophysical Observatory |url=http://www.aras.am/BAO/history.html |website=aras.am |publisher=Armenian Astronomical Society |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160429082053/http://www.aras.am/BAO/history.html |archive-date=April 29, 2016 }} It made Armenia one of the world's centers for the study of [[astrophysics]] in the 20th century.{{sfn|Adalian|2010|p=354}} The [[Orgov Radio-Optical Telescope|ROT-54/2.6]], a [[radio telescope]] built in 1985 by the radiophysicist [[Paris Herouni]] in the village of [[Orgov]], on the slopes of Aragats.{{cite web |last1=Kotlyar |first1=Pavel |title=Война во Вьетнаме выиграна благодаря армянским радиофизикам |url=https://www.gazeta.ru/science/2016/06/14_a_8304977.shtml |website=gazeta.ru |language=ru |date=14 July 2016}} ===Gravity hill=== On the highway leading to fortress Amberd is a [[gravity hill]],{{cite web| url=https://www.armgeo.am/en/gravity-hill-in-aragats/ |title=Mystery of Aragats| website=Armenian Geographic}} which has become a tourist attraction, due to an optical illusion leading to a downhill slope appearing to be uphill. === Mount Aragats hike === Mount Aragats is a popular hiking destination{{Cite web |last=Pahlevanyan |first=Elen |date=January 6, 2022 |title=Top 5 Highest Mountains to Hike in Armenia |url=https://thecascadetravel.com/blog/highest-mountains-to-hike-in-amenia/ |website=thecascadetravel.com |language=English}} among locals and tourists. The southern, lowest peak is the most visited one. The hiking trail is approximately 5 kilometers long, and it typically takes between 2.5 and 3 hours to complete.{{Citation needed|date=September 2023}} ==In culture== [[File:10,000 Armenian dram - 2003 (obverse).png|250px|thumb|The obverse side of the 10,000 [[Armenian dram]] banknote depicts Aragats and poet [[Avetik Isahakyan]].]] Mount Aragats plays a special role in Armenian history and culture. Along with [[Mount Ararat]], it is considered a sacred mountain for the Armenians. Aragats is a [[Armenian name#Given names|male first name]] in Armenia,As of 2022, there are 161 people named Aragats in Armenia's voters list. {{cite web |title=Արագած (Aragats) |url=http://www.anun.am/f/817 |website=anun.am |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230105174609/http://www.anun.am/f/817 |archive-date=5 January 2023 |language=hy}} used especially in areas surrounding the mountain.{{efn|Two examples of notable people named Aragats include Aragats Akhoyan, member of the parliament, born in [[Aghtsk|Dzorap]].{{cite web|title=Aragats Akhoyan|url=http://www.parliament.am/deputies.php?ID=1109&sel=details&lang=eng|website=parliament.am|publisher=National Assembly of the Republic of Armenia}} and Aragats Mkrtchyan, a veteran of the [[First Nagorno-Karabakh War]], from [[Talin, Armenia|Talin]].{{cite web|title=Յուրաքանչյուր մարտ մի քանի րոպեում ես հաղթում. Արագած Մկրտչյան|url=http://razm.info/18691|website=razm.info|publisher=Armenian Ministry of Defense|language=hy|date=23 August 2013}} Both of these settlements are located in the [[Aragatsotn Province]].}}{{Citation needed|date=September 2023}} Mt. Aragats is often associated with [[Gyumri]], Armenia's second-largest city. The mountain is depicted on the coat of arms of Gyumri.{{cite web|title=Symbols of Gyumri|url=http://www.gyumricity.am/index.php/en/gyumri/symbols-of-gyumri|website=gyumricity.am|publisher=Gyumri Municipality|access-date=2016-05-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160325065326/http://www.gyumricity.am/index.php/en/gyumri/symbols-of-gyumri|archive-date=2016-03-25|url-status=dead}} It is also depicted on the obverse side of the 10,000 [[Armenian dram]] banknote (in use since 2003) in the background of [[Avetik Isahakyan]], a poet born in Gyumri.{{cite book|last1=Cuhaj|first1=George S.|title=Standard Catalog of World Paper Money, Modern Issues, 1961-Present|date=2015|publisher=F+W Media, Inc|isbn=9781440244117|page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=h2yYCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA63&dq=Avetik+Isahakyan 63]}} Numerous Armenian poets (e.g., Avetik Isahakyan)[[:hy:s:Արագածին|Արագածին]] have written about Aragats. [[Marietta Shaginyan]] compared Aragats to a "half-open bud of a giant [[pomegranate flower]]".{{cite book|last1=Mikhaĭlov|first1=Nikolaĭ Nikolaevich|title=A Book About Russia: In the Union of Equals: Descriptions, Impressions, the Memorable|date=1988|publisher=Progress Publishers|page=109|quote=Aragats, the highest mountain in Armenia, rises with its split white cone, like the half-open bud of a giant pomegranate flower, to use the words of the well-known Soviet writer Marietta Shaginyan.}} In one short poem, [[Silva Kaputikyan]] compares Armenia to an "ancient rock-carved fortress", the towers of which are Mount Aragats and [[Mount Ararat]]. === In visual art === Numerous artists have painted Aragats. Some examples of paintings of Aragats are kept at the [[National Gallery of Armenia]].{{Citation needed|date=September 2023}} Արագած (1905) Գևորգ Բաշինջաղյան.jpg|[[Gevorg Bashinjaghian]], 1905 Արագած լեռը (1917) Եղիշե Թադևոսյան.jpg|[[Yeghishe Tadevosyan]], 1917 Արագած Փանոս Թերլեմեզյան.jpg|[[Panos Terlemezian]], probably 1941 == Gallery == File:Aragats 2019-05-12.jpg File:Aragats 1112.jpg File:Aragats from Gyumri 1.jpg File:Aragats from mt. {{Short description|Unclimbed mountain in Bhutan}} {{Infobox mountain | name = Gangkhar Puensum | other_name = [[File:Gangkhar Puensum-dz.svg|200px]] | native_name ={{native name|dz|གངས་དཀར་སྤུན་གསུམ་}} | image = gangkhar_puensum_summit.JPG | image_caption =Summit of Gangkhar Puensum | elevation_m = 7571 | elevation_ref =
[[List of highest mountains|Ranked 40th]] | prominence_m = 2995 | prominence_ref =
[[List of peaks by prominence|Ranked 92nd]] | range = [[Himalaya]] | parent_peak = | listing = [[List of countries by highest point|Country high point]]
[[Ultra prominent peak|Ultra]] | location = [[Bhutan]]–[[China]] border | pushpin_map = Bhutan | map_caption = Location of Gangkhar Puensum | image_map = {{OSM Himalaya|lat_d=28.0|long_d=90.5|zoom=7}} | coordinates = {{coord|28|02|54|N|90|27|15|E|type:mountain_scale:100000|format=dms|display=inline,title}} | coordinates_ref = | first_ascent = Unclimbed | easiest_route = }} '''Gangkhar Puensum''' ({{langx|dz|གངས་དཀར་སྤུན་གསུམ་|translit=Kangkar Punsum}}, alternatively, Gangkar Punsum or Gankar Punzum) is the highest mountain in [[Bhutan]] and the [[highest unclimbed mountain]] in the world, with an elevation of {{convert|7570|m|ft|0}} and a [[Topographic prominence|prominence]] of {{convert|2995|m|ft|0}}. In the [[Dzongkha]] language, its name means "White Peak of the Three Spiritual Brothers". Gangkhar Puensum lies on the border between Bhutan and [[Tibet]].{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nj0mEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA13|title=Bhutan|page=13|last1=Cooper|first1=Robert|last2=Yong|first2=Jui Lin|last3=Duling|first3=Kaitlyn|publisher=Cavendish Square Publishing|year=2020|isbn=9781502655769}} After Bhutan was opened for mountaineering in 1983, there were four expeditions that resulted in failed summit attempts in 1985 and 1986. In 1994, Bhutan banned the climbing of peaks over {{convert|6000|m|ft}} and since 2003, all mountaineering has been banned in Bhutan. ==History== [[File:Gangkhar puensum landscape.JPG|right|thumb|The mountain seen from Gophu La pass]] The elevation of Gangkhar Puensum was first measured in 1922, but until recent years, maps of the region were not at all accurate and the mountain was shown in different locations and with markedly different heights. Indeed, because of inadequate mapping, the first team to attempt the summit was unable to find the mountain at all. The book of the 1986 British expedition gives the mountain's height as {{convert|24770|ft|m|0|order=flip}} and states that Gangkhar Puensum is completely inside Bhutan, whereas the nearby [[Kula Kangri]] is completely inside Tibet. Kula Kangri, {{convert|7554|m|ft}}, is a separate mountain {{Convert|30|km|mi|abbr=on|sp=us|sigfig=1}} to the northeast which was first climbed in 1986. It is variously mapped and described as being in Tibet or Bhutan. Since 1994, climbing of mountains in Bhutan above {{Convert|6,000|m|ft|abbr=on|sp=us}} has been prohibited out of respect for local spiritual beliefs.{{Cite book|title=Asian Sacred Natural Sites: Philosophy and practice in protected areas and conservation|last=Verschuuren|first=Bas|publisher=Routledge|year=2016|chapter=Nye within protected areas of Bhutan}} Since 2003, mountaineering has been forbidden completely.{{Cite book|title=A Short History of Asia|last=Mason|first=Colin|publisher=Macmillan International Higher Education|year=2014|isbn=9781137340634|chapter=Nepal and Bhutan}} In 1998, a Japanese expedition secured permission from the Chinese Mountaineering Association to climb the mountain, but permission was withdrawn because of a political issue with Bhutan. This resulted in their permit to climb Gangkhar Puensum itself being revoked.{{Cite web |title=The mountains we have never climbed |url=https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20140703-the-last-mountains-to-climb |access-date=2024-02-25 |website=www.bbc.com}} Instead, in 1999, the team set off from Tibet and successfully climbed [[Liankang Kangri]] (also known as Gangkhar Puensum North), a {{convert|7534|m|ft|0}} subsidiary peak (not an independent mountain), separated from the main peak by a {{convert|2|km|adj=on}} ridge to the north-northwest.{{cite web|url=https://www.peakbagger.com/peak.aspx?pid=35651|access-date=2024-10-30|title=Liangkang Kangri, China/Bhutan|publisher=Peakbagger.com}}{{cite '''Cerro Chirripó''' is the highest mountain in [[Costa Rica]], with an [[elevation]] of 3,821 meters (12,536 feet). It is part of the [[Cordillera de Talamanca]], and the mountain range's highest point. It is located in [[Chirripó National Park]] and is noted for its ecological wealth. 

Mount Chirripó is very tall relative to its surroundings, evidenced by its particularly high [[topographic prominence]] of {{Convert|3727|m|ft|0|abbr=on}}.<ref name="PeakList">{{Cite web |url=http://www.PeakList.org/WWlists/ultras/CentAm.html |title=Central America ultra-prominent peaks |publisher=PeakList.org |access-date=2007-04-07}}</ref> This makes it the [[List of peaks by prominence|37th most prominent peak]] in the world. On clear days it is possible to see across the country from the [[Pacific Ocean]] to the [[Caribbean Sea]].<ref name="distance">{{Cite web |url=http://costa-rica-guide.com/Natural/Chirripo.html |title=Chirripó National Park |publisher=costa-rica-guide.com |access-date=2010-02-10}}</ref>
==Geography==
Chirripó is the [[List of peaks by prominence|37th most prominent peak]] in the world. The most abundant [[ecosystem]] in the mountains is the [[Costa Rican páramo|páramo]], which extends across almost all the mountains. It also has a large number of lakes on the top, which is because during the previous [[ice age]] it was covered with snow. When the ice melted, these unique [[Glacial lake|glacial lakes]] were formed. The mountain was named "Chirripo", meaning "land of eternal waters", by [[Indigenous peoples of Costa Rica|indigenous Costa Ricans]] because of the many lakes and streams around the mountain.<ref>{{Cite web |title=All About Chirripó |url=http://www.hikingchirripo.com/all-about-chirripo |website=www.hikingchirripo.com}} {{dead link|date=March 2024}}</ref>

===Climate===
The temperatures on Mount Chirripo during the day range between {{Convert|4|and|18|C}}, and at night they can drop to between {{Convert|-3|and|1|C}}. The coldest temperature ever documented in Costa Rica was {{Convert|-9|C}}, and recorded here. [[Snow]] has not fallen on the peak in the past 100 years or so, but [[hail]] is sometimes reported.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Stokes |first=Maya F. |last2=Goldberg |first2=Samuel L. |last3=Perron |first3=J. Taylor |date=2018 |title=Ongoing River Capture in the Amazon |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1029/2018GL078129 |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |language=en |volume=45 |issue=11 |pages=5545–5552 |doi=10.1029/2018GL078129 |issn=1944-8007|hdl=1721.1/140798.2 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==History==
The earliest known civilization to inhabit the area of Chirripó was the indigenous [[Cabécar people|Cabécar]] people. In 1904, [[Agustín Blessing Presinger]] became the first known European to climb the peak. 

The first official hiking trail was constructed in 1965; it led to a small sheet-metal hut five kilometers away from the peak. Today, the hut has been replaced by a concrete building visited by 7,000 people each year. In 1975, Chirripó National Park was founded, enclosing and protecting 500 square kilometers of rain forest and mountains around the peak.<ref name="Mit Press">{{Cite book |title=Wild Costa Rica: the wildlife & landscapes of Costa Rica |last=Hepworth |first=Adrian |date=2008 |publisher=[[MIT Press]] |isbn=9780262083836}}</ref>

Since 1953, there have been five major [[wildfire]]s in the area. Forest fires occurred in 1976,<ref name="First Fire">{{Cite web |url=http://www.infocostarica.com/places/chirripo_hp.html |title=First Fire |last=Harry Pariser |publisher=Explore Costa Rica |access-date=2010-02-10 |archive-date=February 8, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090208224521/http://www.infocostarica.com/places/chirripo_hp.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> in the 1990s,<ref name="Second Fire">{{Cite web |url=http://meghanjoyward.wordpress.com/2009/06/13/cerro-chirripo-12530-feet/ |title=Second Fire (Weak) |publisher=blog on wordpress.com |access-date=2010-02-10}}</ref> and in 2012.<ref name="Brigadistas combaten últimas llamas en el Chirripó">{{Cite web |url=http://www.nacion.com/2012-03-10/Sucesos/brigadistas-combaten-ultimas-llamas-en-el-chirripo.aspx |title=Brigadistas combaten últimas llamas en el Chirripó |last=David Delgado |publisher=Diario La Nación |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120310222044/http://www.nacion.com/2012-03-10/Sucesos/brigadistas-combaten-ultimas-llamas-en-el-chirripo.aspx |archive-date=2012-03-10 |access-date=2012-03-10}}</ref>

==Ecology==
In the lowest parts of the mountains, the [[cloud forest]] dominates, with [[oak]] trees no higher than 50 meters, accompanied with [[mosses]], [[lichen|lichens]], and [[orchids]]. Whereas, in the upper parts of the mountain the [[Costa Rican páramo|páramo]] is predominant, an ecosystem characterized by short and dry grass. The high peaks in Chirripó National Park and [[La Amistad International Park]] host important areas of [[Talamancan montane forests|Talamancan montane forest]] and [[Costa Rican Páramo]] with high [[Endemic (ecology)|endemism]] and extremely high [[biodiversity]]. The peaks of these mountains constitute [[sky island]]s for many species of plants and animals. In fact, types of [[squirrels]], [[hummingbirds]], [[rabbits]], [[resplendent quetzal|quetzals]], [[frogs]], [[white-nosed coati]] and even [[jaguars]] habit the mountains.

==Hiking==
A permit from the National Park office in [[San Gerardo de Rivas]] is needed to climb Mount Chirripó. The summit can be reached from the trailhead via a 19.5-kilometer (12.1 mile) hike,<ref>{{Cite web |title=notes on climbing Chirripo |url=http://www.peakbagging.com/Chirripo.html |access-date=2011-04-09 |publisher=peakbagging.com}}</ref> which starts 1,500 meters (4,900 ft) above sea level in the village of [[San Gerardo de Rivas|San Gerardo]] in the [[Talamanca Range]]. From the valley, the path rises through fields, woodlands, and eventually [[Talamancan montane forests|lush rainforest]]. The forest gradually turns into scrubland. The trail continuously ascends and descends through ridges and valleys until it reaches the final visitors' refuge at an elevation of 3,392 meters, from which there is a two hour hike to the summit. Once the last ridge is crossed, 200 meters of steep path lead up to the summit, which is a 6-meter wide platform of rocks.<ref name="Mit Press" />

{{short description|Tallest mountain in Peru}} {{use dmy dates|date=August 2025}} {{Infobox mountain | name = Huascarán | image = Nevado Huascarán (south view).jpg | image_caption = Huascarán as viewed from [[Cordillera Negra]] | elevation_m = 6768 | elevation_ref = {{cite book|last=Helman|first=Adam|title=The Finest Peaks: Prominence and Other Mountain Measures|year=2005|isbn=978-1-4120-5995-4|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LUmA5yY1F_YC&pg=PA5|page=5|publisher=Trafford }} | prominence_m = 2776 | prominence_ref = {{cite web|url=http://www.peaklist.org/WWlists/ultras/peru.html |title=ultra-prominences|publisher=peaklist.org|access-date=2008-12-29}} | range = [[Cordillera Blanca]], Andes | listing = [[List of countries by highest point|Country high point]]
[[Ultra prominent peak|Ultra]] | location = [[Yungay province|Yungay]], Peru | pushpin_map = Peru | range_coordinates = | map_caption = Peru | map_size = 240 | coordinates = {{coord|09|07|18|S|77|36|15|W|type:mountain_region:PE_scale:100000|format=dms|display=inline,title}} | coordinates_ref = | topo = | type = [[Granite]] | age = [[Cenozoic]] | first_ascent = {{ubl|Huascarán Sur: 20 July 1932|Huascarán Norte: 2 September 1908}} | easiest_route = glacier/snow/ice climb }} '''Huascarán''' ({{IPA|es|waskaˈɾan}}; [[Quechuan languages|Quechua]]: '''Waskaran'''), '''Nevado Huascarán''' or '''Mataraju''' is a [[mountain]] located in [[Yungay Province]], Ancash Department, Peru. It is situated in the [[Cordillera Blanca]] range of the western [[Andes]]. The southern summit of Huascarán ({{Lang|es|Huascarán Sur}}), which reaches {{convert|6768|m|0}}, is the highest point in [[Peru]], the northern Andes (north of [[Lake Titicaca]]), and in all of the Earth's [[tropics]]. It is the fourth highest mountain in [[South America]] after [[Aconcagua]], [[Ojos del Salado]], and [[Monte Pissis]]. Huascarán is ranked 25th by [[topographic isolation]]. == Names == [[File:Mount Huascaran viewed from Yungay, Peru (cropped).jpg|thumb|View of Huascarán from the town of [[Yungay, Peru|Yungay]]]] Until the 20th century, the mountain lacked a single commonly accepted name and was known by different names within the surrounding towns and villages. The first recorded mention of the name {{Lang|es|Huascarán}} appeared in 1850 as ''Huascan'',{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/mountainnames0000july|url-access=registration|title=Mountain names|last=Julyan|first=Robert Hixson|date=1984-09-01|publisher=Mountaineers|isbn=978-0-89886-091-7|language=en}} given by the local people likely because the mountain rises above the village of Huashco. Huashco got its name from the [[Quechuan languages|Quechua]] word for rope ({{Lang|qu|waska}}). At the beginning of the 20th century, the name appeared as {{Lang|es|Huascarán}}, and has not changed since.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=H80nAQAAIAAJ|title=Andean Air Mail & Peruvian Times|date=1967|publisher=Andean Air Mail & Peruvian Times|language=en}} It seems that {{Lang|es|Huascarán}} is merely a contraction of {{Lang|qu|Huashco-Urán}}, or 'beyond and down from the village of Huashco'.{{Cite web|url=http://publications.americanalpineclub.org/articles/12196606300/Quechua-Names-in-the-Northern-Peruvian-Andes-and-Their-Meanings|title=Quechua Names in the Northern Peruvian Andes and Their Meanings - AAC Publications - Search The American Alpine Journal and Accidents|website=publications.americanalpineclub.org|access-date=2020-01-06}} Other names given to the mountain are ''Matarao'' and ''Mataraju'', the latter being the name that local indigenous people prefer to call it,{{Cite web|url=https://issuu.com/gibergarcia/docs/6._1907_-_enock_-_the_andes_and_the/273|title=Enock. "The andes and the amazon", 1907.|website=Issuu|date=3 February 2018 |language=en|access-date=2020-01-06}} from [[Ancash Quechua]] {{Lang|qu|mata}} ('twin') and {{Lang|qu|rahu}} ('snow peak'), meaning 'twin snow peaks'. == Myth == According to a legend, Huascarán was a nobleman who lived in a certain place in [[Department of Ancash|Áncash]], while [[Huandoy]] was a woman who lived in a small town very close to where that mountain is. Huascarán was enormously in love with the woman, and they always saw each other secretly. One day Huascarán's father found out that he was in love with the lowborn woman, so he asked the [[Inti|Sun God]] for help. Seeing that he could not separate the two lovers, he decided to turn them into mountains, but the divinity decided to bring them together so that despite being mountains they continued with their love.{{nosource|date=November 2023}} ==Geography== The mountain has two distinct summits, the higher being the south one ({{Lang|es|Huascarán Sur}}) with an elevation of {{convert|6768|m|0}}. The north summit ({{Lang|es|Huascarán Norte}}) has an elevation of {{convert|6654|meters|0}}. The two summits are separated by a [[Saddle (landform)|saddle]] called {{Lang|es|la Garganta}}. The core of Huascarán, like much of the Cordillera Blanca, consists of [[Cenozoic]]-age [[granite]].Ricker, John F., ''Yuraq Janka: Cordilleras Blanca and Rosko'', Alpine Club of Canada, 1977, {{ISBN|0-920330-04-5}}, after Wilson, Reyes, and Garayar, 1967. Huascarán gives its name to [[Huascarán National Park]] which surrounds it, and is a popular location for trekking and [[mountaineering]]. The mountain's summit is one of the farthest points on the Earth's surface from its center,{{cite web|url=http://www.abc.net.au/science/k2/moments/s1086384.htm|title=Tall Tales about Highest Peaks|date=16 April 2004|publisher=Australian Broadcasting Corporation|access-date=2008-12-29}} closely behind the farthest point at [[Chimborazo]] in [[Ecuador]]. It is also the place on Earth with the smallest [[Gravity of Earth|gravitational force]],{{cite web|title=Gravity Variations Over Earth Much Bigger Than Previously Thought|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2013/09/130904105345.htm|date=September 4, 2013|publisher=Science Daily|access-date=2014-01-01}} with an estimated acceleration of 9.76392 m/s2.{{cite journal |last1=Hirt |first1=Christian |last2=Claessens |first2=Sten |last3=Fecher |first3=Thomas |last4=Kuhn |first4=Michael |last5=Pail |first5=Roland |last6=Rexer |first6=Moritz |date=28 August 2013 |title=New ultrahigh-resolution picture of Earth's gravity field: New Picture of Earth's Gravity Field |url=https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/grl.50838 |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |language=en |volume=40 |issue=16 |pages=4279–4283 |doi=10.1002/grl.50838 |hdl=20.500.11937/46786 |s2cid=54867946 |access-date=13 January 2023 |hdl-access=free}} == Climbing == [[File:Mirador del Huascarán.jpg|thumb|The mountain is easily seen from the surrounding area, with viewing spots ({{Lang|es|miradores}}) found alongside the road to the mountain]] Huascarán is normally climbed from the village of Musho to the west via a high camp in the {{Lang|es|Garganta}} [[col]]. The ascent normally takes five to seven days, the main difficulty being the large [[crevasse]]s that often block the route.Biggar, John The normal route is of moderate difficulty and rated between PD and AD (depending on the conditions of the mountain) according to the [[International French adjectival system|International French Adjectival System]]. === History === The summit of {{Lang|es|Huascarán Sur}} was first reached on 20 July 1932 by [[Erwin Schneider]], {{ill|Hermann Hoerlin|de}}, Franz Bernard, Phillip Borchers, Erwin Hein who were members of a joint [[Germany|German]]–[[Austria]]n expedition.{{cite web archived|url=http://www.huascaranperu.net/Ascenciones.htm |title=1932 ascent |publisher=huascaranperu.net |access-date=2014-07-01 |url-status=dead |archive-date=February 15, 2012 }}{{cite journal | title = In the Cordillera Blanca ; the 1932 D .ce Oe. A.-V. Expedition | journal =Alpine Journal| date= 1933| first = Philip | last =Borchers | issn= 0065-6569 |volume =#45 | pages=34–44 | access-date =4 December 2025 |url = https://www.alpinejournal.org.uk/Contents/Contents_1933_files/AJ45%201933%2034-44%20Borchers%20Cordillera%20Blanca.pdf }} The team followed what would later become the normal route (the {{Lang|es|Garganta}} route). The north peak ({{Lang|es|Huascarán Norte}}) had previously been climbed on 2 September 1908 by a [[United States|U.S.]] expedition that included [[Annie Smith Peck]],{{cite web|url=http://www.ric.edu/faculty/rpotter/smithpeck.html|title=Annie Smith Peck|publisher=Dr. Russell A. Potter|access-date=2010-12-05}} though this first ascent is somewhat disputed. In 1989, a group of eight [[amateur]] mountaineers, the "Social Climbers", held what was recognized by the ''[[Guinness Book of Records]]'' (1990 edition) to be "the world's highest dinner party" on top of the mountain, as documented by [[Chris Darwin]] and [[John Amy]] in their book ''The Social Climbers'', and raised [[British pound|£]]10,000 for charity.{{cite book | title=ABC de la evolución | first=Julián | last=Monge-Nájera | publisher=EUNED | year=1995 | isbn=9977-64-822-0 | page=58 }}{{cite news | url=http://www.guardian-series.co.uk/news/1705342.mouthwatering_challenge/ | journal=Epping Forest Guardian | title=Mouth-watering challenge | date=21 September 2007 | access-date=2011-05-31 }} On 20 July 2016, nine climbers were caught in an [[avalanche]] on Huascarán's normal route at approximately {{convert|5800|m||abbr=on}}, four of whom died.{{cite web|url=http://amountainjourney.com/mountain-climbers-avalanche-huascaran-andes-peru/|title=Avalanche On Huascaran In Andes Of Peru Kills 4, 5 Rescued - A Mountain Journey|work=A Mountain Journey | Backcountry Skiing, Climbing, Mountaineering, Hiking |date=21 July 2016|access-date=12 June 2018}} On 9 July 2024, it was reported that the body of William Stampfl, an American mountaineer, had been found 22 years after he disappeared in an avalanche in June 2002.{{Cite web |date=2024-07-09 |title=American mountaineer found mummified in Peru 22 years after vanishing |url=https://gulfnews.com/world/americas/american-mountaineer-found-mummified-in-peru-22-years-after-vanishing-1.1720511963353 |access-date=2024-07-09 |website=gulfnews.com |language=en}} The body of one of Stampfl's climbing companions had previously been recovered. A third member of the group is still unaccounted for.{{Cite news |last1=Zhuang |first1=Yan |last2=Taj |first2=Mitra |date=2024-07-10 |title=22 Years Ago, He Disappeared in an Avalanche. His Body Was Just Found. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/07/10/world/americas/22-years-ago-he-disappeared-in-an-avalanche-his-body-was-just-found.html |access-date=2024-07-10 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} === Huascarán Norte === Apart from the normal route, climbed in 1908 and rated PD+/AD-, all the other routes are committing and serious. # Northwest ridge (Italian route), rated ED1/ED2 climbed on 25 July 1974 by E. Detomasi, C. Piazzo, D. Saettone and T. Vidone. # Northwest face (Polish–Czech variant), rated ED1/ED2, climbed on 14 July 1985 by B. Danihelkova, [[Zuzana Hofmannová|Z. Hofmannová]], A. Kaploniak, E. Parnejko and E. Szczesniak. # North face (Paragot route), rated ED1, climbed on 10 July 1966 by R. Paragot, R. Jacob, C. Jacoux and D. Leprince-Ringuet. # North face (Swiss route), rated ED2+, climbed on 23 May 1986 by D. Anker and K. Saurer. This route requires at least four days on the face. # North face (Spanish route), rated ED2+, climbed on 20 July 1983 by J. Moreno, C. Valles and J. Tomas. === Huascarán Sur === As for the South summit, apart from the normal route all the others are difficult. # West ridge (Shield route), rated D+, climbed on 15 June 1969 by W. Broda, S. Merler and B. Segger. Approach as for the Garganta route but then the route develops over the knife-edge West ridge before getting to the summit icefield. # West ridge direct (Lomo fino route), rated TD-, was climbed on 7 July 2007 by M. Ybarra and S. Sparano. Approach as for the Garganta route but afterwards the route develops straight over the West face. # Northeast ridge (Spanish route), rated TD+, was climbed on 18 July 1961 by F. Mautino, P. Acuna, A. Perez and S. Rivas. The route starts from Chopicalqui col, crosses the upper part of the Matara glacier and reaches the northeast ridge developing across cornices and snow mushrooms. == 1970 earthquake == [[File:Yungay avalanche labels.jpg|thumb|right|Photograph taken after the 1970 avalanche showing the buried towns of Yungay and Ranrahirca]] {{main|1970 Huascarán debris avalanche}} On 31 May 1970, the [[1970 Ancash earthquake|Ancash earthquake]] caused a substantial part of the north side of the mountain to collapse in an avalanche with an estimated {{convert|80|e6m3||abbr=off}} of ice, mud and rock, measuring about {{convert|0.5x1|mi||1|order=flip}}. It advanced about {{convert|11|mi|km|order=flip|abbr=on}} at an average speed of {{convert|280|to|335|km/h|abbr=on|round=5}},{{cite journal|url=http://www.iris.edu/seismo/quakes/1970peru/Plafker1971.pdf|title=Geological Aspects of the May 31, 1970 Peru Earthquake|journal=Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America|date=June 1971|volume=61|issue=2|pages=543–578|doi=10.1785/BSSA0610030543|s2cid=130140366|access-date=2014-01-01|last1=Plafker |first1=George |last2=Ericksen |first2=George E. |last3=Fernández Concha |first3=Jaime |bibcode=1971BuSSA..61..543P }} burying the towns of [[Yungay, Peru|Yungay]] and [[Ranrahirca]] under ice and rock, killing more than 20,000 people.{{cite journal|last=U.S. Dept. of the Interior|date=October 1970|title=The Peru Earthquake: a Special Study|journal=Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists|volume=26|issue=8|pages=17–19 |doi=10.1080/00963402.1970.11457853|bibcode=1970BuAtS..26h..17.}}{{cite web archived |url=http://www.jayfrogel.com/Peru98/Peru98_Yungay/0Peru98_Yungay_home.html |title=The Village of Yungay and the Surrounding Countryside |publisher=Jay A. Frogel |archive-date=2012-02-18 |access-date=2010-12-05}} At least 20,000 people were also killed in [[Huaraz]],{{Dubious|reason=No deaths in [[Huaraz]] are mentioned in the article on the [[1970 Huascarán Debris Avalanche]]|date=June 2025}} the site of a 1941 avalanche (see [[Lake Palcacocha]]).{{Needs independent confirmation|reason=The cited 48 page crude PowerPoint (Huascaran.ppt) by Mark W Williams (https://snobear.colorado.edu) includes no citations|date=June 2025}} Estimates suggest that the earthquake killed over 66,000 people.Gates & Ritchie p. 110{{cite book|title=Peru|year=2004|publisher=Lonely Planet|first1=Rob|last1=Rachowiecki|first2=Charlotte|last2=Beech|page=308}} The final toll was 67,000 dead and 800,000 homeless, making it the worst earthquake-induced disaster in the [[Western Hemisphere]] until the [[2010 Haiti earthquake]]. Also buried by an avalanche was a [[Czechoslovakia|Czechoslovak]] mountaineering team, none of whose 15 members were ever seen again.{{cite web archived |title=Historie československé expedice Peru 1970 (Czech only) |url=http://www.hkvysehrad.cz/peru70.html |archive-date=2014-07-09 |access-date=2015-09-14 |url-status=dead}} This and other earthquake-induced avalanche events are often described{{By whom|date=November 2017}} as "eruptions" of Huascarán, despite not being of volcanic origin. An earlier avalanche on 10 January 1962, caused by a rapid rise in temperature,{{cite web archived|url=http://snobear.colorado.edu/Markw/Mountains/07/Andes/Huascaran.ppt|title=Sacred mountains: Myth and Morphology|access-date=2014-01-01|archive-date=2021-04-13|url-status=dead}} killed an estimated 4,000 people.{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/onthisday/hi/dates/stories/january/11/newsid_3306000/3306665.stm|title=1962: Thousands killed in Peru landslide|publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation|access-date=2010-12-05|date=1962-01-11}} ==Ice Coring== In the early 1990s, scientific campaigns were launched to drill [[ice cores]] at Huascarán. During a scouting mission in 1991, a network of stakes was established to monitor snow accumulation rates on the mountain [[col]].{{cite journal |last1=Davis |first1=M. E. |last2=Thompson |first2=L. G. |last3=Mosley-Thompson |first3=E. |last4=Lin |first4=P. N. |last5=Mikhalenko |first5=V. N. |last6=Dai |first6=J. |title=Recent ice-core climate records from the Cordillera Blanca, Peru |journal=Annals of Glaciology |date=1995 |volume=21 |pages=225–230 |doi=10.3189/S026030550001586X}} In 1993, researchers from the [[Byrd Polar and Climate Research Center]] returned to drill two ice cores down to bedrock—approximately 160 meters below the surface.{{cite journal |last1=Thompson |first1=L. G. |last2=Mosley-Thompson |first2=E. |last3=Davis |first3=M. E. |last4=Lin |first4=P. -N. |last5=Henderson |first5=K. A. |last6=Cole-Dai |first6=J. |last7=Bolzan |first7=J. F. |last8=Liu |first8=K. -b. |title=Late Glacial Stage and Holocene Tropical Ice Core Records from Huascarán, Peru |journal=Science |date=1995 |volume=269 |issue=5220 |pages=46–50 |doi=10.1126/science.269.5220.46}} The climate records preserved in the deepest ice layers are at least 19,000 years old. Following a new scouting mission to Huascarán in 2016,{{cite journal |last1=Thompson |first1=L. G. |last2=Davis |first2=M. E. |last3=Mosley‐Thompson |first3=E. |last4=Beaudon |first4=E. |last5=Porter |first5=S. E. |last6=Kutuzov |first6=S. |last7=Lin |first7=P.‐N. |last8=Mikhalenko |first8=V. N. |last9=Mountain |first9=K. R. |title=Impacts of Recent Warming and the 2015/2016 El Niño on Tropical Peruvian Ice Fields |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres |date=2017 |volume=122 |issue=23 |doi=10.1002/2017JD026592}} researchers returned to Huascarán in 2019 to drill two new ice cores to bedrock on the Huascarán col, extending the record of the original ice cores by 26 years.{{cite journal |last1=Weber |first1=A. M. |last2=Thompson |first2=L. G. |last3=Davis |first3=M. |last4=Mosley‐Thompson |first4=E. |last5=Beaudon |first5=E. |last6=Kenny |first6=D. |last7=Lin |first7=P.‐N. |last8=Sierra‐Hernández |first8=R. |title=Drivers of δ18O Variability Preserved in Ice Cores From Earth's Highest Tropical Mountain |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres |date=2023 |volume=128 |issue=19 |doi=10.1029/2023JD039006|doi-access=free }} In addition to the new col ice cores, the researchers also drilled two ice cores to bedrock on Huascarán Sur. Because the south summit of Huascarán is the highest peak in Earth’s tropics, the ice cores from Huascarán Sur are the highest-elevation tropical ice cores ever collected. ==See also==
