Khan Tengri.wikitext:
{{Short description|Mountain on the China–Kazakhstan–Kyrgyzstan tripoint}} {{refimprove|date=July 2025}} {{Infobox mountain | name = Khan Tengri | image = Vue globale du versant N du khan Tengri.jpg | image_caption = Khan Tengri above North [[Engilchek Glacier]] | elevation_m = 7010 | elevation_ref = {{cite opentopomap|Khan Tengri|42.21072|80.17445|2023-06-30}} | prominence_m = 1685 | prominence_ref = {{cite web|url=http://www.peaklist.org/WWlists/ultras/StansP1500m.html|title=The Central Asian Republics: Ultra-Prominence Page|website=peaklist.org|access-date=2014-05-26}} This prominence figure is based on the elevation of 6995m. | range = [[Tian Shan]] | listing = [[List of elevation extremes by country|Country high point]]
[[Ultra-prominent peak|Ultra]] | location = [[Ak-Suu District]], [[Issyk-Kul Region]], Kyrgyzstan
[[Raiymbek District]], [[Almaty Region]], Kazakhstan
[[Wensu County]], [[Xinjiang]], China | pushpin_map = Asia#Kyrgyzstan#Kazakhstan#China#China Xinjiang | map_caption = Location in Asia, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, China, and its Xinjiang Province respectively | pushpin_label_position = left | coordinates = {{coord|42|12|39|N|80|10|30|E|type:mountain_scale:100000|format=dms|display=inline,title}} | coordinates_ref = | topo = | type = | age = | first_ascent = 1931 Mikhail Pogrebetsky | easiest_route = glacier/snow/ice/rock climb | other_name = Hantengri Peak }} '''Khan Tengri''' is a [[mountain]] of the [[Tian Shan]] [[mountain range]] in [[Central Asia]]. It is on the [[China]]—[[Kyrgyzstan]]—[[Kazakhstan]] [[tripoint]], east of lake [[Issyk-Kul|Issyk Kul]] in Kyrgyzstan. Its geologic elevation is {{convert|6995|m|ft|0|abbr=on}}, but its glacial icecap rises to {{convert|7010|m|ft|0|abbr=on}}. For this reason, in mountaineering circles, including for the [[Snow Leopard award]] criteria, it is considered a 7,000-metre peak. Khan Tengri is the second-highest mountain in the [[Tian Shan]], surpassed only by [[Jengish Chokusu]] (meaning 'Victory Peak' in the [[Kyrgyz language]], formerly known as Peak Pobeda) (7,439 m). Khan Tengri is the highest point in [[Kazakhstan]] and third-highest peak in Kyrgyzstan, after [[Jengish Chokusu]] (7,439 m) and [[Lenin Peak|Avicenna Peak]] (7,134 m). It is also the world's most northern 7,000-metre peak, notable because peaks of high latitude have a shorter climbing season and generally more severe weather. ==Names== The name "Khan Tengri" literally means 'King Heaven' in [[Kyrgyz language|Kyrgyz]] and [[Kazakh language|Kazakh]] or 'King Sky' in [[Mongolian language|Mongolian]] and possibly references the [[sky deity]], [[Tengri]], that exists both in the religion of [[Tengrism]] and [[Buddhism in Central Asia|Central Asian Buddhism]]. In some other local languages, it is known as ''Khan Tangiri Shyngy'', ''Kan-Too Chokusu'', ''Pik Khan-Tengry'', and ''Hantengri Feng''. ({{langx|mn|Хан Тэнгэр}}, {{langx|kk|Хан Тәңірі|Han Täñırı }}, حان تأڭئرئ; {{langx|ky|Хан-Теңири}} Han-Teñiri, حان-تەڭىرى; {{Langx|ug|خانتەڭرى}}; {{zh|s=汗腾格里峰|t=汗騰格里峰|p=Hànténggélǐ Fēng}}, [[Xiao'erjing]]: هًا تٍْ قْ لِ فعْ). Local residents named the mountain Khan Tengri for the unique beauty of snow giants.{{cn|date=July 2025}} ==Features== Khan Tengri is a massive marble pyramid, covered in snow and ice. At sunset the marble glows red, giving it the name "blood mountain" in Kazakh and Kyrgyz ({{langx|kk|Қантау}}; {{langx|ky|Кан-Тоо}}). Located just across the South [[Engilchek Glacier|Engilchek]] (or Inylchek) glacier, 16 km north of [[Jengish Chokusu]], Khan Tengri was originally thought to be the highest peak in the Tian Shan because of its dramatic, steep shape, compared to the massive presence of Jengish Chokusu. This perception was probably also due to Khan Tengri's visibility across the plains of southern Kazakhstan while Jengish Chokusu remains out of view of civilization. Khan Tengri is the highest peak in the rugged Tengri Tag subrange, also known as the Mustag, that also contains [[Chapaev Peak]] ({{cvt|6371|m|disp=semicolon}}) and Gorky Peak ({{cvt|6050|m|disp=semicolon|0}}). [[Anatoli Boukreev]] considered Khan Tengri perhaps the world's most beautiful peak because of its geometric ridges and its symmetry. ==History== Although it is almost {{convert|430|m|ft|abbr=on}} lower than its neighbor, Khan Tengri was believed to be the highest peak in the range until [[Jengish Chokusu]] was surveyed in 1943 and determined to be higher. [[Pyotr Semyonov-Tyan-Shansky|Peter Semenov]] was the first European to see the Tengri Tag and its peak, the colossal Khan Tengri (in 1857).Semenov, Petr Petrovitch. ''Travels in the Tian'-Shan' 1856-1857''. Trans. by Liudmila Gilmour, Colin Thomas and Marcus Wheeler. Edited and annotated by Colin Thomas, pp. 180, 184-185. The Hakluyt Society, London. (1998). {{ISBN|0-904180-60-3}}. The first ascent of the peak was made in 1931 by {{Interlanguage link|Mikhail Pogrebetsky|lt=Mikhail Pogrebetsky's|kk|Михаил Тимофеевич Погребецкий}} Ukrainian team through a route from the south (Kyrgyzstan side), then along the west ridge. M. Kuzmin's team made the first ascent from the north (Kazakhstan side) in 1964. Khan Tengri is one of five peaks that a Soviet mountaineer needed to scale to earn the prestigious [[Snow Leopard award]]. [[Anatoli Boukreev]] achieved the first solo speed ascent in 1990.{{citation needed|date=April 2019}} A team from Kazakhstan made the first winter ascent of Khan Tengri on February 7, 1992; the team included [[Valery Khrichtchatyi]], Viktor Dedi, Yuri Moiseyev, Valdimir Suviga, Aleksandr Savin, Igor Putintsev and Malik Ismetov.{{cite journal|url=http://publications.americanalpineclub.org/articles/12199329401/Asia-CISKirgizia-Khan-Tengri-Tien-Shan-First-Winter-Ascent|title=Khan Tengri, Tien Shan, First Winter Ascent|journal=[[American Alpine Journal]]|year=1993|access-date=2023-06-30}}{{cite journal|url=http://www.alpinejournal.org.uk/Contents/Contents_1995_files/AJ%201995%20255-263%20Russia%20Central%20Asia.pdf|title=Russia and Central Asia 1992-1994|journal=[[Alpine Journal]]|year=1995|page=259|access-date=2023-06-30}} Austrian mountaineer and expedition leader [[Toni Dürnberger]] died while descending after having climbed Khan Tengri on August 17, 1992.[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HujXbsAXJZM Video in Gedenken an den österreichischen Bergsteiger Toni Dürnberger] In 2004, more than a dozen mountaineers were killed in a large avalanche on the Pogrebetsky route, the most popular route on the mountain. The peak appears on the 100 [[Kyrgyzstani som|Kyrgyz som]] note. {{gallery |align=center |Image:South Inylchek Base Camp.jpg |South Inylchek Base Camp, at 4,000 m on the glacier's southern moraine, looking northwest to [[Chapaev Peak]] and Khan Tengri in the distance |Image:KyrgyzstanP21-100Som-2002 b.jpg |The peak appears on the 100 [[Kyrgyzstani som|Kyrgyz som]] note |Image:Xinjiang DSC 8179 (3813626261).jpg |Khan Tengri and [[Jengish Chokusu]] as seen from Chinese Provincial Road S313 }} == See also== * [[List of ultras of Central Asia]] ==Footnotes== {{Reflist}} ==External links== * {{cite summitpost|id=150339|title=Khan Tengri}} * {{cite peakware|id=137|name=Khan Tengri}} * [https://web.archive.org/web/20170202190920/http://mountains.tos.ru/breef.htm#pobeda Khan Tengri route maps] * [https://kantengri.kz/en/tours/mountaineering International Mountaineering Camp Kan Tengri] * [https://eu.zonerama.com/Album/d42cbc79-57b9-434a-831b-f41dc4136ac0 Photo-story of Czech climber Petr Podruh] {{Kazakhstan topics}} {{Highest points of Asia}} {{Highest points of Europe}} {{Authority control}} [[Category:Mountains of China]] [[Category:Mountains of Kazakhstan]] [[Category:Mountains of Kyrgyzstan]] [[Category:Issyk-Kul Region]] [[Category:Landforms of Almaty Region]] [[Category:Kazakhstan–Kyrgyzstan border]] [[Category:International mountains of Asia]] [[Category:Seven-thousanders of the Tian Shan]] [[Category:China–Kazakhstan border]] [[Category:China–Kyrgyzstan border]] [[Category:Border tripoints]] [[Category:Highest points of countries]] [[Category:Tengriism]] [[Category:Pyramidal peaks]] [[Category:Ultra-prominent peaks of Asia]]

{{Short description|Highest mountain in Venezuela}} {{For|the peak named after Bolívar in Colombia|Pico Simón Bolívar}} {{Infobox mountain | name = Pico Bolívar | image = PicoBolivar2.jpg | image_caption = Peak Bolívar during snow season | elevation_m = 4978 | elevation_ref = | prominence_m = 3957 | prominence_ref = {{cite web |title=Venezuela, Guianas, and Brazil Ultra-Prominences - peaklist.org |url=http://peaklist.org/WWlists/ultras/ven_bra.html |website=peaklist.org |access-date=2013-02-12 |quote=The prominence value given here is based on an elevation of 4,981 m.}}

[[Ultra prominent peak|Ultra]] | location = [[Mérida, Mérida]], [[Venezuela]] | range = [[Sierra Nevada de Mérida|Sierra Nevada]], [[Andes]] | coordinates = {{coord|08|32|30|N|71|02|45|W|type:mountain_scale:100000|format=dms|display=inline,title}} | coordinates_ref = | first_ascent = 1935 by Enrique Bourgoin, H. Márquez Molina and Domingo Peña }} '''Pico Bolívar''' is the highest mountain in [[Venezuela]], at 4,978 metres (16,332 ft).{{cite web |last1=Pérez |first1=Omar J. |last2=Hoyer |first2=Melvyn |last3=Hernández |first3=José N. |last4=Rodríguez |first4=Carlos |last5=Márques |first5=Víctor |last6=Sué |first6=Nicolás |last7=Velandia |first7=José R. |last8=Deiros |first8=Diego |title=Alturas del Pico Bolívar y otras cimas andinas venezolanas a partir de observaciones Gps |url=http://www.scielo.org.ve/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S0378-18442005000400005&lng=es&nrm=iso |website=Interciencia v.30, n.4, Caracas |access-date=2012-09-27 |pages=213–216 |language=es |date=September 2005}} Located in [[Mérida State]]. It can be reached only by walking; the [[Mérida cable car]], which was the highest and longest cable car in the world when it was built, only reaches [[Pico Espejo]]. From there it is possible to climb to Pico Bolívar. The peak is named after the Venezuelan independence hero [[Simón Bolívar]]. The Pico Bolívar is located on the mountain previously called La Columna, next to El León (4,743 m) and El Toro (4,695 m). The new name was suggested by [[Tulio Febres Cordero]] in 1925. It was officially renamed on December 30, 1934. == Elevation == The height of this prominent Andean peak has been estimated and calculated various times during history. In 1912, one [[triangular]] measurement pointed at {{convert|5,002|m}}. In 1928 came another calculation at {{convert|5,007|m}}, which stood as official height for a long time. During the 1990s, the scientists Heinz Saler and Carlos Abad calculated the height, based upon [[GPS]] observations to be {{convert|4,980.8|m}}.{{cite web |author1=Figueredo, Ivarelys |title=Venezuela Innovadora |url=http://www.venezuelainnovadora.gov.ve/noticias_2002/noti_nov35.html |website=www.venezuelainnovadora.gov.ve |via=web.archive.org |publisher=El Nacional/ Venezuela Innovadora |access-date=29 May 2024 |date=9 February 2006 |language=es |archive-date=9 February 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060209022832/http://www.venezuelainnovadora.gov.ve/noticias_2002/noti_nov35.html |url-status=dead }} New GPS measurements were made in 2002, which stated a height of 4,978.4 ±0.4 metres. These more correct findings were published in 2005. The final measurement was made by José Napoleón Hernández from IGVSB; Diego Deiros and Carlos Rodriguez from USB and two guides from Inparques. GPS measurements designed for geodetic network consists of the vertices Pico Bolívar, El Toro, Piedras Blancas, and Mucuñuque Observatory, the latter belonging to the Venezuelan Red Geocentric REGVEN. Measurements were temporally equally long and continuous to ensure a greater volume of data over time to make more consistent and reliable information, five (5) GPS dual frequency receivers were used.{{cite web |url=https://archive.org/stream/IGVSBBG142003/IGVSB-BG-14-2003#page/n3/mode/2up |title=Boletín Geográfico IGVSB-BG No 14 |work=IGVSB: PUBLIC CATALOGUE - NATIONAL LIBRARY OF VENEZUELA |via=archive.org |access-date=29 May 2024}} [[Image:Bolívar Peak Massif.svg|thumb|upright=3.5|center|Panoramic of Bolívar Peak. Ascent route Bourgoin - Peña]] {{Clear}} ==Glacial retreat== [[File:Pico Bolívar 1950-2011.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|Comparison between the mountain's glacier, 1950 and 2011 respectively.]] During the [[Merida glaciation]] in the [[Pleistocene epoch]], the glaciated area had a maximum extent of 600 km2 and covered mountains with a height of at least {{convert|3000|m|abbr=on}}. At the end of the glaciation, the area covered by the glaciers progressively shrank, and before the start of the [[Little Ice Age]] they had possibly all disappeared.{{citation needed|date=December 2012}} It is estimated that in 1910 the area covered by glaciers was around {{convert|10|km2|abbr=on}}, divided in two large areas, one embracing Picos Bolívar, Espejo and Concha and the other embracing Picos Humboldt and Bonpland. Possibly a small glaciated area covered the northwest side of Pico El Toro.{{Cite web |url=http://www.saber.ula.ve/bitstream/123456789/26199/1/articulo22.pdf |title=Efectos del calentamiento global ¿Nieves eternas en la Sierra Nevada de Mérida? |website=www.saber.ula.ve |language=es}} [[File:Pico Simón Bolívar.jpg|left|thumb|Pico Bolívar shrouded in clouds]] Aerial pictures taken in 1952 show the glaciated area had already shrunk to {{convert|0.9|km2|abbr=on}} for the Picos Bolívar, Espejo and Concha and to {{convert|2.0|km2|abbr=on}} for the Picos Humboldt and Bonpland. In 2003 almost all the glaciers of the area had disappeared, with the exception of two small glaciated areas ({{convert|7.48|ha|abbr=on}} on Pico Bolívar and {{convert|35.81|ha|abbr=on}} on Pico Humboldt).{{citation needed|date=December 2012}} By 2012, the glaciers on Pico Bolivar had disappeared, and by May 2024, the glaciers on Pico Humboldt disappeared as well, making Venezuela one of the first countries to lose all its glaciers.{{Cite web |last=Telemundo |first=Noticias |last2=Linares |first2=Albinson |date=2024-05-25 |title='A great sadness': Venezuela is first Andean country to lose of all its glaciers |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/latino/-great-sadness-venezuela-first-andean-country-lose-glaciers-rcna153784 |access-date=2024-05-27 |website=NBC News |language=en}} [[File:PicoBolivar3.jpg|thumb|upright=3|center|Panoramic view of Pico Bolívar.]] {{Clear}} ==References== * Pérez O, Hoyer M, Hernández J, Rodríguez C, Márques V, Sué N, Velandia J, Deiros D. (2005). "Alturas del Pico Bolívar y otras cimas andinas venezolanas a partir de observaciones GPS" ''Interciencia''. 30 (4). [https://web.archive.org/web/20061107030719/http://redalyc.uaemex.mx/redalyc/pdf/339/33910305.pdf] * Jahn, A. "Observaciones glaciológicas de los Andes venezolanos" ''Cult. Venez.'' 1925, 64:265-80 ==Notes== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{Portal|Andes}} * [http://www.peakbagger.com/peak.aspx?pid=8344 "Pico Bolívar, Venezuela" on Peakbagger] {{Commons category}} {{Andean glaciers}} {{Authority control}}{{Highest points of South America}}{{DEFAULTSORT:Pico Bolivar}} [[Category:Mountains of Venezuela|Bolivar]] [[Category:Glaciers of Venezuela]] [[Category:Geography of Mérida (state)]] [[Category:Highest points of countries]] [[Category:Four-thousanders of the Andes]] [[Category:Sierra Nevada National Park (Venezuela)]] [[Category:Extreme points of Venezuela]]

Almer, J. Cockin and C. Shkhara is the highest peak of the [[Greater Caucasus Mountains|Greater Caucasus Mountain Range]] since both [[Elbrus]] and [[Dykhtau]] are located along the side ranges, which lie to the north of it. Shkhara lies {{Convert|88|km|mi|0}} north of [[Kutaisi]], Georgia's third-largest city, and right at the townlet of [[Mestia]]. The summit lies in the central part of the [[Caucasus Mountains|Greater Caucasus Mountain Range]], south-east of [[Mount Elbrus]], [[Europe]]'s highest mountain. Shkhara is the third-highest peak in the [[Caucasus]], just behind [[Dykh-Tau]].[https://www.mountain-forecast.com/peaks/Shkhara/forecasts/5200 Shkhara. Weather Forecast, Georgia] mountain-forecast.com == Morphology == Shkhara is the high point and the eastern anchor of a [[massif]] known as the [[Bezengi Wall]], a {{Convert|11-12|km|mi|-long|adj=mid}} ridge. It is a large, steep peak in a heavily glaciated region, and presents serious challenges to mountaineers. Its north face (on the Russian side) is {{Convert|1500|m|ft|-2}} high and contains several classic difficult routes. The significant sub-summit Shkhara West, at {{Convert|5068|m|ft|0|abbr=on}}, is a climbing objective in its own right, and a traverse of the entire Bezingi Wall is considered "Europe's longest, most arduous, and most committing expedition". == History == The peak was first climbed in 1888 via the North East Ridge route, by the [[United Kingdom|British]]/[[Switzerland|Swiss]] team of English climber [[John Garforth Cockin]] and Swiss guides [[Ulrich Almer]] and [[Christian Roth (mountaineer)|Christian Roth]].J. Mafadi.description: Peak on the border of South Africa and Lesotho
Mafadi.wikitext:
{{Short description|Peak on the border of South Africa and Lesotho}} {{Use South African English|date=August 2026}} {{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}} {{Infobox mountain | name = Maifadi | image = | image_caption = | elevation_m = 3446.1 | elevation_ref = | pushpin_map = South Africa#Lesotho | map_caption = Location of Maifadi in South Africa (on border with Lesotho) | map_size = 225 | pushpin_label_position = right | listing = [[List of countries by highest point|Country high point]]

A morning thunderstorm approaches from the North West. Champagne's Castle (South Africa's third highest mountain at 3377m) visible on the horizon. Also the prominent Cathkin Peak in the center of the photo. Below the escarpment, clouds cover the valleys of the lower Drakensberg (South Africa).]] '''Maifadi''' is a peak on the border of South Africa and Lesotho. At a height of {{convert|3446.1|m|ft}},{{sfn|Slingsby|1983}} it is the highest mountain in the nation of South Africa, but is lower than [[Thabana Ntlenyana]], the highest peak in [[Lesotho]] which is, at {{convert|3482|m|ft}}, the highest point in [[Southern Africa]]. By the Himalayan definition of a mountain, being a summit with at least 7% topographic prominence relative to height, Maifadi is not in fact a mountain summit, but rather a subsidiary summit of Makheka in Lesotho.{{Cite web|title=Mafadi - Peakbagger.com|url=https://www.peakbagger.com/peak.aspx?pid=17493|access-date=2022-02-02|website=www.peakbagger.com}} By this definition, [[Champagne Castle]] is the highest mountain summit in South Africa, although Maifadi is unquestionably the highest point in South Africa. == Ascent== ===Hiking=== Ascents of Maifadi, attempted from the South African side, are normally made from the [[Njesuthi]] campsite. The [[Njesuthi]] escarpment of the Drakensberg is one of the more remote hiking regions, and normally takes two days to reach the escarpment. The route involves about an {{convert|8|km}} hike to Marble Baths. This is followed by continuing up the river and with a combination of short paths and boulder hopping. This all ends at the bottom of the ridge, which leads to the Molar, with a campsite. The subsequent path up the ridge to the top of the mountains is known as Leslie's Pass. The path follows the ridge until below a rocky band where it traverses to southern side. The way continues up a short scree section, followed by more hiking up a quite steep gradient, until the final {{convert|20|m}} are made up a grassy slope. From here, the top of Leslie's Pass{{efn|Leslie's Pass {{coord|29|09|12.7|S|29|20|38.0|E|name= Leslie's Pass|display=inline|type:landmark_region:ZA}} }} follows, and a spectacular hike up the ridge connecting Lithobolong and Maifadi. A route referred to as the Corner-Leslies Loop is becoming a popular way of reaching Maifadi. It entails hiking to Centenary Hut in Injisuthi Nature Reserve on day 1, ascending Corner Pass and climbing Maifadi on day 2, descending Leslie's Pass to Marble Baths on day 3, and returning to the [[Njesuthi]] campsite on day. ===Running=== On 8 October 2015, South African trail runners [[Ryan Sandes]] and [https://www.instagram.com/ryno_griesel/?hl=en Ryno Griesel] set a Fastest Known Time (FKT) for the ascent of Mafadi via the Northern High Approach, an alternative, and slightly shorter but steeper route of the popular Corner's pass. They set a time of 5h 47.59 min, starting and ending at the [[Njesuthi]] campsite, and covered a total of {{convert|38.52|km}} with approximately {{convert|2400|m}} of elevation gain/loss. The previous FKT was set in 2012 by fellow South African, Andrew Porter, with a time of 6 h 22 min from the Giant's Castle campsite via Judge pass. == Disputed name == The name of Maifadi (which literally means the Mother of Fadi) is currently under dispute, its original Sotho name Ntheledi (which means "Makes me slip", referring to the nearby stream) being considered by some to be more relevant and correct.{{sfn|Wimber|2011|pp=107-113}} ==See also== *[[List of mountains in South Africa]] ==References== {{Notelist}} {{Reflist|refs= {{Cite {{lang|ar|جَبَل حَضُوْر}} | image = Haraz 200612 Yemen-117 (353667919).jpg | image_size = 300px | image_caption = Jabal An-Nabi Shu'ayb, a peak in the [[Jabal Haraz|Haraz Mountains]], near [[Sanaa]] in Yemen | elevation_m = 3666 | elevation_ref = [http://www.peaklist.org/WWlists/ultras/mideast.html "Arabian peninsula and Middle East"] Peaklist.org. [[Ultra prominent peak|Ultra]], Ribu | location = [[Sanaa Governorate]], [[Yemen]] | range = [[Jabal Haraz|Haraz]]-[[Sarawat Mountains]] | coordinates = {{coord|15|16|45|N|43|58|33|E|type:mountain_scale:100000|format=dms|display=inline,title}} | coordinates_ref = | topo = | type = | age = | last_eruption = | first_ascent = | easiest_route = }} '''Jabal An-Nabī Shuʿayb''' ({{langx|ar|جَبَل ٱلنَّبِي شُعَيْب|lit=Mountain of the Prophet Shuaib}}), also called '''Jabal Hadhur''' ({{langx|ar|جَبَل حَضُوْر|link=no|Jabal Ḥaḍūr}}),{{Cite book |last=زبارة |first=محمد بن محمد بن يحيى اليمني/الصنعاني |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=L4dyDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT359 |title=نيل الوطر من تراجم رجال اليمن في القرن الثالث عشر 1-2 ج1 |date=1998-01-01 |publisher=Dar Al Kotob Al Ilmiyah (دار الكتب العلمية) |isbn=978-2-7451-2623-8 |language=ar}}{{cite book |publisher=[[Qatar Digital Library]] |title=Gazetteer of Arabia |volume=II [1044] (81/688) |url=https://www.qdl.qa/en/archive/81055/vdc_100023727632.0x000052 |year=1917 |access-date=2020-04-17}}{{cite web |publisher=Mindat.org |title=Jabal an-Nabī Shu'ayb, Bani Matar, Sanaa, Yemen |url=https://www.mindat.org/feature-72377.html |access-date=2020-04-17}} is a 3,666 meter high mountain in the [[Jabal Haraz|Haraz]]i subregion of the [[Sarawat Mountains|Sarawat]], located in [[Bani Matar District]], [[Sanaa Governorate]], [[Yemen]]. It is the highest mountain in the country and the [[Arabian Peninsula]].{{cite book |author=Robert D. Burrowes |title=Historical Dictionary of Yemen |pages=5–340 |publisher=[[Rowman & Littlefield]] |year=2010 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tjXRfqBv_0UC |isbn=978-0-8108-5528-1}}{{cite book |last=McLaughlin |first=Daniel |title=Yemen |publisher=[[Bradt Travel Guides]] |chapter=1: Background |page=3 |isbn=978-1-8416-2212-5 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eQvhZaEVzjcC |year=2008}} It is the 62nd most [[prominence|prominent]] peak in the world, and the [[List of Ultras of West Asia|third most prominent in the Middle East]]. == Name == The mountain is named after a [[Prophets and messengers in Islam|prophet]] called ''Shuʿayb ibn Mahdam ibn Dhī-Mahdam al-Ḥaḍūrī'' ({{lang|ar|شُعَيْب ابْن مَهْدَم ابْن ذِي مَهْدَم ٱلْحَضُوْرِي}}). According to Islamic scholars, he is different from [[Shuaib]] of [[Midian]]. According to Al-Hamdani, he was sent to the people of Mikhlaf Hadhur, but they killed him, and [[God in Islam|God]] sent Bakht Nasr, who destroyed their town.{{Cite book|last=حسين|first=فرح، محمد|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=y_GmnOZajl4C|title=الجديد في تاريخ دولة وحضارة سبأ وحمير: معالم تاريخ اليمن الحضاري عبر ٩٠٠٠ سنة|date=2004|publisher=وزارة الثقافة والسياحة،|pages=716|language=ar}}{{Cite book|last=العزيز|first=البكري/أبو عبيد عبد الله بن عبد|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cCd0DwAAQBAJ|title=معجم ما استعجم من أسماء البلاد والمواضع 1-3 مع الفهارس ج1|date=1998-01-01|publisher=Dar Al Kotob Al Ilmiyah دار الكتب العلمية|isbn=978-2-7451-0035-1|pages=90|language=ar}} Locals believe that his tomb is on the mountain.{{Cite book|last=الهمدانى|first=ابى محمد الحسن بن احمد بن يعقوب|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8SsqDgAAQBAJ&pg=PT127|title=صفة جزيرة العرب|date=1990|publisher=ktab INC.|language=ar}} The mountain is also called ''Jabal Hadhur'' because it is located in the region of Mikhlaf Hadhur. == Description == The height of the mountain is {{convert|3,666|m|ft|0}}. Although its elevation is often reported to be {{convert|3,760|m|ft|abbr=off}}, this is not supported by [[SRTM]] data or more recent cartographic sources.[http://www.pbase.com/bmcmorrow/image/41334608 Map at pbase.com] Retrieved 2011-11-20 The mountain is located near the Yemeni capital city of [[Sanaa]], and rises from about {{convert|1,500|–|1,600|m|ft|abbr=on}}. The western side of the mountain blocks rain clouds, a [[rain shadow]] effect causing that side to be relatively fertile. Atop the mountain is a military post with radar, as well as the purported shrine to [[Shuaib]]. File:Haraz 200612 Yemen-115 (353667843).jpg|The mountain (background) as viewed from the terraced side of mountain at [[Al Mahwit Governorate]] File:Kawkaban -68 (353668857).jpg|As viewed from [[Kawkaban]] in Al-Mahwit Governorate === Climbing === Although the summit is not snow-capped like its counterparts in northern [[Lebanon]] and [[Syria]], there have been reports of snow on the peak and frost in the winter. Wind speeds are very high at the summit.{{citation needed|date=November 2018}} In April 2019, Ahmad Zein Al-Yafei, an [[Emirati people|Emirati]] security officer from [[Dubai]], claimed that he [[Mountaineering|scaled the mountain]] in 69 hours, unfurling the banner of the [[Dubai Police Force|Dubai Police]] at the peak.{{cite news |newspaper=[[Gulf News]] |title=Dubai security officer scales Jebel An-Nabi Shu'ayb |location=[[Dubai]] |url=https://gulfnews.com/uae/dubai-security-officer-scales-jebel-an-nabi-shuayb-1.63177391 |date=2019-04-07 |access-date=2020-04-15}} === Geology === The mountain is a prominent part of the tertiary volcanic series, which builds up large parts of the Yemeni highlands. Its rocks were sampled, analyzed and studied in detail by the German mineralogist [[Dieter R. Fuchs]]. He elaborated in depth the geochemistry and petrogenetic properties and elaborated a thesis on the formation of this geological series.{{cite thesis|title=Doctoral Thesis of Dieter R. Fuchs|periodical=|publisher=|url=http://d-nb.info/861054695|url-status=|format=|access-date=|archive-url=|archive-date=|last=|date=|year=|language=|pages=|quote=|last1=Fuchs|first1=Dieter}} ==See also== * [[List of ultras of West Asia]] * [[South Arabia]] ** [[Geography of Yemen]] ** [[Geology of Yemen]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== * [https://peakery.com/jabal-an-nabi-shuayb-yemen/ Jabal an-Nabi Shu'ayb] * [http://www.peakbagger.com/peak.aspx?pid=10477 Jabal an-Nabī Shu‘aib, Yemen] * [http://www.mountain-forecast.com/peaks/Jabal-an-Nabi-Shu-ayb/forecasts/3666 Forecast for Jabal An-Nabi Shu'ayb] * [https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/highest-mountains-in-yemen.html Highest Mountains In Yemen] * [http://www.marsnjak.com/sergej/?menu=yemen&pic=628&type=pic&zoom=1 Jabal an-Nabi Shu'ayb - The highest mountain] * [https://www.pbase.com/bmcmorrow/image/41332228 Village at the base of Jabal an-Nabi Shu'ayb] * [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DsUGWdiOrQA اعرف بلدك: جبل النبي الشعيب.. أعلى قمة جبلية في الشرق الأوسط] ([[YouTube]], in Arabic) * [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZNRCpNTvymo أين يقع جبل النبي شعيب] * [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HIl2g7Vg1V4 النزول من جبل النبي شعيب] {{Mountains in the Arabian Peninsula}} {{Highest points of Asia}} [[Category:Mountains of Yemen|Nabi Shuayb]] [[Category:Highest points of countries]] [[Category:Bani Matar district]] [[Category:Ultra-prominent peaks of Asia]]

{{short description|Mountain on Iraq and Iran border}} {{Infobox mountain | name = Cheekha Dar | image = Cheekhedar.jpg | image_caption = | elevation_m = 3611 | elevation_ref = {{cite peakbagger|pid=13186|name=Cheekha Dar, Iraq/Iran|accessdate=2014-05-26}} | prominence_m = 1575 | prominence_ref = | pushpin_map = Iraq | map_caption = Location of Cheekah Dar in Kurdistan-Iraq(on the Iranian border) | map_size = 250 | pushpin_label_position = bottom | listing = [[List of countries by highest point|Country high point]]
[[Ultra prominent peak|Ultra]] | location = [[Iran]]–[[Iraq]] border | range = [[Zagros Mountains]] | coordinates = {{coord|36|46|36|N|44|55|07|E|type:mountain_scale:100000|format=dms|display=inline,title}} | coordinates_ref = | first_ascent = }} '''Cheekha Dar''' ({{langx|ku|Çîxî Derê}}, {{langx|ckb|چیخی دەرێ}}), which means Black Tent, is the local Kurdish name for the mountain, located in Kurdistan Region of Iraq, currently thought to be the highest in [[Iraq]]. It is claimed to be {{cvt|3,611|m}} high in the [[The World Factbook|CIA World Factbook]].{{cite web |title=The World Factbook — Central Intelligence Agency |url=https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/the-world-factbook/fields/2020.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070613003330/https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/the-world-factbook/fields/2020.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 13, 2007 |website=www.cia.gov}} It is {{cvt|6|km}} north of the village of Gundah Zhur and is on the border with [[Iran]]. == History == It was climbed in November 2004 by English explorer [[Eamon Ginge Fullen|Ginge Fullen]], who recorded a GPS reading of 3,628 meters at the coordinates in the adjacent table. The location is consistent with [[SRTM]] and Russian topographic mapping, although these sources are more consistent with the [[CIA]] height. The first reported winter ascent was by Jonathan Beswick and Matthew DuPuy on March 18, 2011. The expedition GPS confirmed {{cvt|3,611|m}}. There is a danger of [[land mine]]s in the area on approach between [[A. M. Hamilton#Hamilton Road|Hamilton Road]] and the village of Gundah Zhur. Some fields are marked by red, triangular signs with skull and crossbones. It is possible to find Kurdish military escorts through this area in the town of Choman. A nearby peak called [[Halgurd]] is around {{cvt|3,607|m}} high, and was previously thought to be Iraq's highest mountain. == See also == * [[Iraqi Kurdistan]] * [[List of elevation extremes by country]] ==References== {{Reflist}} {{highest points of Asia}} [[Category:Mountains of Iraq]] [[Category:Mountains of Kurdistan]] [[Category:International mountains of Asia]] [[Category:Iran–Iraq border]] [[Category:Highest points of countries]] [[Category:Mountains of Kurdistan Province]] [[Category:Mountains of Iran]] {{Iraq-geo-stub}}

The [[China–Mongolia border|international border]] between [[China]] and [[Mongolia]] runs across its summit point, which, at {{Convert|4356|m}}, is the highest point in the Altais and the highest in both Mongolia and [[Altay Prefecture]] in [[Western China]]. The peak is covered in snow year-round. In the past, Khüiten Peak was also officially known in [[Mongolia]] as the "Friendship Peak" ({{langx|mn|link=no|Найрамдал уул}}, {{IPA|mn|ˈnæe̯ɾə̆mtɬ ˈoːɬ|pron}}).See e.g. the index in {{harvnb|Krumwiede|Kamp|Leonard|Kargel|2014}}; or see the Soviet [http://www.mountain.ru/world_mounts/altai/2006/M45-104.jpg Topo map M45-104], scale 1:100,000, where the name Mt. Nairamdal (г. Найрамдал) is associated with the peak whose elevation is 4374.0 m. The highest peak is also referred to as Nairamdal in {{harvnb|Chistyakov|Ganiushkin|2015|p=209}} Khüiten Peak is one of five peaks of the [[Tavan Bogd]] [[massif]]. 1962 by Harrer, Temple, Kippax, and Huizenga | easiest_route = rock/snow/ice climb }} [[File:Carstenzs from other side.jpg|thumb|Puncak Jaya region icecap, [[Papua (province)|Papua]]]] '''Puncak Jaya''' ({{IPA|id|ˈpuntʃak ˈdʒaja|lang}}; literally 'Victorious Peak', {{langx|uhn|Nemangkawi Ninggok}}){{Cite book |author=Müller, Kal |title=Amungme : tradition and change in the highlands of Papua |date=2008 |publisher=Freeport Indonesia |oclc=316516243 }} or '''Carstensz Pyramid''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|k|ɑr|s|t|ən|s}}, {{langx|id|Piramida Carstensz}}, {{langx|nl|Carstenszpiramide}}) on the island of [[New Guinea]], with an elevation of {{convert|4884|m|abbr=on}}, is the [[list of islands by highest point|highest mountain peak of an island]] on Earth, and the highest peak in Indonesia and within [[Oceania]]. The mountain is located in the [[Sudirman Range]] of the highlands of [[Mimika Regency]], [[Central Papua]], Indonesia. Puncak Jaya is ranked 5th in the world by [[topographic isolation]]. When regarding New Guinea as part of the [[Australia (continent)|Australian continent]] in a biogeographical sense, Puncak Jaya can be considered the [[List of highest points of Oceanian countries|highest peak in all of Oceania]], with its elevation exceeding those of the highest peaks in the nearby nations of Papua New Guinea ([[Mount Wilhelm]]), New Zealand ([[Aoraki / Mount Cook]]) and Australia ([[Mount Kosciuszko]]). Puncak Jaya is therefore often listed as one of the [[Seven Summits]]. However, since Puncak Jaya is in [[Western New Guinea]], an area administered by Indonesia and therefore geopolitically part of [[Southeast Asia]], the peak can also be considered the [[List of Southeast Asian mountains|8th highest mountain]] in this region, after [[Hkakabo Razi]] and six others in [[Kachin State]], Myanmar. The massive, open cut [[Grasberg mine|Grasberg]] gold and copper mine, the world's [[list of largest gold mines by production|second-largest gold mine]], is {{convert|4|km|mi|spell=in}} west of Puncak Jaya. Other summits are ''[[Carstensz East|East Carstensz Peak]]'' ({{cvt|4808|m|||disp=sqbr}}), ''[[Sumantri]]'' ({{cvt|4870|m|||disp=sqbr}}) and ''[[Ngga Pulu]]'' ({{cvt|4863|m|||disp=sqbr}}). Other names include '''Nemangkawi''' in the [[Amung language|Amungkal]] language, '''Carstensz Toppen''' and '''Gunung Soekarno'''.Greater Atlas of the World, Mladinska knjiga, Ljubljana, Slovenia, 1986. It is also the highest point between the [[Himalayas]] and the [[Andes]].{{clarify|date=November 2025}} ==Etymology== The name of the mountain in the indigenous [[Amung people|Amungme]] peoples' language is Nemangkawi Ninggok meaning Peak of the White Arrow. The name Puncak Jaya is [[Indonesian language|Indonesian]] for 'Glorious Peak'. It is also known as the Carstensz Pyramid, Mount Jayawijaya, or Mount Carstensz. ==History== The highlands surrounding the peak were inhabited before European contact, and the peak is known as '''Nemangkawi''' in [[Amung language|Amungkal]]. ===Dutch discovery=== Puncak Jaya was named "Carstensz Pyramid" after [[Dutch Republic|Dutch]] explorer [[Jan Carstenszoon]], who was the first [[Europe]]an to sight the [[glacier]]s on the peak of the mountain on a rare clear day in 1623.{{cite book | last = Neill | first = Wilfred T. | author-link = Wilfred T. Neill | title = Twentieth-Century Indonesia | url = https://archive.org/details/twentiethcentury0000neil | url-access = registration | publisher = [[Columbia University Press]] | year = 1973 | page = [https://archive.org/details/twentiethcentury0000neil/page/14 14] | isbn = 978-0-231-08316-4}} The sighting went unverified for over two centuries, and Carstensz was ridiculed in Europe when he said he had seen snow near the [[equator]]. It appeared on maps of the time as ''Sneebergh.''{{Cite web |url=https://nla.gov.au/nla.obj-232563272 |title=Wilhelm and Johan Blaeu, India quae orientalis dicitur, et insulae adiacentes, Amsterdam, 1664 |access-date=16 April 2022 |archive-date=5 October 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241005162439/https://nla.gov.au/nla.obj-232563272/view |url-status=live }} The [[snowfield]] of [[Puncak Trikora]], {{cvt|170.|km}} east of here, was reached as early as 1909 by a Dutch explorer, [[Hendrik Albert Lorentz]], with six of his [[Dayak people|Dayak]] [[Kenyah people|Kenyah]] porters recruited from the [[Apo Kayan]] in [[Borneo]].Lorentz, H.A., 1910. Zwarte Menschen – Witte Bergen: Verhaal van den Tocht naar het Sneeuwgebergte van Nieuw-Guinea, Leiden: [[Brill Publishers|EJ. Brill.]] The predecessor of the [[Lorentz National Park]], which encompasses the Carstensz Range, was established in 1919 following the report of this expedition. [[File:Puncak Jaya glaciers 1850-2003 evolution map-fr.gif|thumb|right|Animated map of the extent of the glaciers of the Carstensz Range from 1850 to 2003.]] ==Geology== Puncak Jaya is the highest point on the [[New Guinea Highlands|Central Range]], which was created in the late [[Miocene]] [[Melanesian orogeny]],{{cite journal|last1=Dow|first1=D.B.|author2=Sukamto R.|year=1984|title=Late Tertiary to Quaternary Tectonics of Irian Jaya|journal=Episodes|volume=7|issue=4|pages=3–9|doi=10.18814/epiiugs/1984/v7i4/001|doi-access=free}} that was caused by an oblique collision between the [[Australian Plate|Australian]] and [[Pacific Plate|Pacific]] plates, and is made of middle Miocene [[limestone]]s.{{cite journal|last1=Weiland|first1=Richard J.|first2=Mark|last2=Cloos|title=Pliocene-Pleistocene asymmetric unroofing of the Irian fold belt, Irian Jaya, Indonesia: Apatite fission-track thermochronology|journal=[[Geological Society of America|GSA Bulletin]]|year=1996|volume=108|issue=11|pages=1438–49|doi=10.1130/0016-7606(1996)108<1438:ppauot>2.3.co;2|bibcode=1996GSAB..108.1438W}} ===Glaciers=== [[File:Puncak Jaya icecap 1936.jpg|thumb|left|Puncak Jaya icecap 1936]] [[File:Puncak Jaya icecap 1972.jpg|thumb|left|Puncak Jaya icecap 1972]] While Puncak Jaya's peak is free of ice, there are several [[glaciers]] on its slopes, including the [[Carstensz Glacier]], [[West Northwall Firn]], [[East Northwall Firn]] and the recently vanished [[Meren Glacier]] in the Meren Valley (''meren'' is Dutch for "lakes").{{cite web |last1=Kincaid |first1=Joni L. |last2=Klein |first2=Andrew G |year=2004 |title=Retreat of the Irian Jaya Glaciers from 2000 to 2002 as Measured from IKONOS Satellite Images |url=https://www.easternsnow.org/s/16-Kincaid-Klein.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241005162426/https://www.easternsnow.org/s/16-Kincaid-Klein.pdf |archive-date=5 October 2024 |access-date=3 November 2011 |work=61st Eastern Snow Conference |pages=147–157}} Being equatorial, there is little variation in the mean temperature during the year (around {{cvt|0.5|C|disp=sqbr|F|}}) and the glaciers fluctuate on a seasonal basis only slightly. However, analysis of the extent of these rare equatorial glaciers from historical records show significant retreat since the 1850s, around the time of the Little Ice Age Maximum which primarily affected the Northern Hemisphere, indicating a regional warming to around {{cvt|0.6|C|F||}} over more than a century between 1850 and 1972. The glacier on [[Puncak Trikora]] in the [[Maoke Mountains]] disappeared completely some time between 1939 and 1962.{{cite web |author1=Allison, Ian |author2=Peterson, James A. |title=Glaciers of Irian Jaya, Indonesia and New Zealand |url=https://pubs.usgs.gov/prof/p1386h/indonesia/indonesia.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080512011301/http://pubs.usgs.gov/prof/p1386h/indonesia/indonesia.html |archive-date=12 May 2008 |access-date=2018-09-06 |work=U.S. Geological Survey, U.S.Department of the Interior}} Since the 1970s, evidence from satellite imagery indicates the Puncak Jaya glaciers have been retreating rapidly. The Meren Glacier melted away sometime between 1994 and 2000. An expedition led by paleoclimatologist [[Lonnie Thompson]] in 2010 found that the glaciers are disappearing at a rate of {{convert|7|m|spell=in||}} thickness per year and in 2018 they were predicted dynamics.png|alt=|thumb|Disappearance of glaciers from Puncak Jaya, 1984–2020]] ==Climbing== {{More citations needed section|date=August 2018}} [[File:Puncak Jaya (NASA astronaut photograph).jpg|thumb|The highland area in 2005, with the [[Grasberg mine|Grasberg copper mine]] pit in the foreground. Its summit is at the far end of the central rib.]] Puncak Jaya is one of the more demanding climbs in one version of the [[Seven Summits]], despite having the lowest elevation. It is held to have the highest technical rating, though not the greatest physical demands of that list's ascents. The standard route to climb the peak from its base camp is up the north face and along the summit ridge, which is all hard rock surface.{{Cite web|url=http://xtremesport4u.com/extreme-land-sports/the-most-technical-of-the-7-summits/|title=The most technical of the 7 summits|last=Jones|first=Lola|date=15 December 2009|website=Xtreme Sport|access-date=13 June 2016|archive-date=24 June 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160624004738/http://xtremesport4u.com/extreme-land-sports/the-most-technical-of-the-7-summits/|url-status=live}} Despite the large [[Grasberg mine|mine]], the area is highly inaccessible to hikers and the general public. The standard route to access base camp as of 2013 is to fly into the nearest major town with an airport, [[Timika]], and then take a small aircraft over the mountain range and onto an unimproved runway at one of the local villages far down from the peak. It is then typically a five-day hike via the Jungle route to the base camp through very dense rainforest and with regular rainfall, making the approach probably the "most miserable" of the Seven Summits. Rain during most days of the hike inbound and out are not uncommon. Unlike the other Seven Summits, if one sustains an injury on the inbound hike, there is little or no ability to get rescued via helicopter. Anyone injured must evacuate by foot over very difficult and slippery terrain. The descent from the peak's base camp can take three to four days. Anecdotally, it appears most injuries occur during the descent due to a combination of exhaustion and difficulty controlling hiking speed on the wet and slippery terrain. An additional complication is relatively common work strikes by the climbing porters that accompany most expeditions, occasionally halting their work to demand (and usually receive) higher pay before agreeing to continue. The one-day summit bid is technically challenging for those with little rock climbing experience, and it can be quite cold with temperatures at or below freezing near the summit. Patches of snow sometimes appear on the route up or on the ropes of the [[Tyrolean traverse]] just below the summit. ===Climbing history=== [[File:Carstensz-expeditie.jpg|thumb|left|Left to right: [[Anton Colijn]], [[Frits Wissel]] and [[Jean Jacques Dozy]] during the [[Carstensz expedition]] in 1936.]] In 1936, the Dutch [[Carstensz expedition]], unable to establish definitively which of the three summits was the highest, attempted to climb each. [[Anton Colijn]], [[Jean Jacques Dozy]], and [[Frits Wissel]] reached both the glacier-covered East Carstensz and Ngga Pulu summits on December 5, but, due to bad weather, failed in their attempts to climb the bare Carstensz Pyramid. Because of extensive snow melt, Ngga Pulu has become a {{cvt|4862|m}} subsidiary peak, but it has been estimated that in 1936 (when glaciers still covered {{cvt|13|km2}} of the mountain; see map) Ngga Pulu was indeed the highest summit, reaching over {{cvt|4900|m|-2}}.[http://www.knag.nl/index.php?id=640&tx_ttnews%5Bswords%5D=gis&tx_ttnews%5Bpointer%5D=100&tx_ttnews%5Btt_news%5D=132&tx_ttnews%5BbackPid%5D=502&cHash=bc09ff844a Interview with Jean Jacques Dozy] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120331060530/http://www.knag.nl/index.php?id=640&tx_ttnews%5Bswords%5D=gis&tx_ttnews%5Bpointer%5D=100&tx_ttnews%5Btt_news%5D=132&tx_ttnews%5BbackPid%5D=502&cHash=bc09ff844a|date=31 March 2012}} in 2002 (in Dutch). The now-highest Carstensz Pyramid summit was not climbed until 1962, by an expedition led by the Austrian mountaineer [[Heinrich Harrer]], New Zealand mountaineer [[Philip Temple]], Australian rock climber Russell Kippax, and Dutch patrol officer Albertus (Bert) Huizenga. Temple had previously led an expedition into the area and pioneered the access route to the mountains.{{cite web |author=Temple, Philip |date=4 October 2013 |title=Account of first ascent |url=http://climbcarstensz.wordpress.com/2013/10/04/punjak-jaya-mountain-of-the-imagination-an-account-of-the-first-ascent-of-carstensz-pyramid-by-philip-temple/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140520221256/http://climbcarstensz.wordpress.com/2013/10/04/punjak-jaya-mountain-of-the-imagination-an-account-of-the-first-ascent-of-carstensz-pyramid-by-philip-temple/ |archive-date=20 May 2014 |access-date=7 January 2021}} When Indonesia took control of the province in 1963, the peak was renamed Poentja' Soekarno (Simplified [[Indonesian language|Indonesian]]: Puncak Sukarno) or Sukarno Peak, after the then-[[President of Indonesia]] [[Sukarno]]; later this was changed to Puncak Jaya due to the subsequent [[de-Sukarnoization]]. ''Puncak'' means peak or mountain and ''Jaya'' means 'victory', 'victorious', or 'glorious'. The name Carstensz Pyramid is still used among [[mountaineering|mountaineers]].{{cite book |last1=Parfet |first1=Bo |title=Die Trying: One Man's Quest to Conquer the Seven Summits |last2=Buskin |first2=Richard |publisher=[[American Management Association]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-8144-1084-4 |place=New York, N.Y. |page=178}} ===Access=== Access to the peak requires a government permit. The mountain was closed to tourists and climbers between 1995 and 2005. As of 2006, access is possible through various adventure tourism agencies.{{cite web |title=Cartensz Pyramid |url=http://7summits.com/carstensz/carstensz.php |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060716130532/http://7summits.com/carstensz/carstensz.php |archive-date=16 July 2006 |access-date=7 July 2006 |publisher=7summits.com}} Despite being among the lowest of the Seven Summits, Puncak Jaya is considered to be a technically difficult climb, requiring extensive planning, acclimatisation, mountaineering skills, and support services, due to its remoteness and sheer limestone faces. Located in an isolated area of central Papua, there are no nearby facilities, and climbers have the option to take a helicopter to the base camp and reach the summit within three to four days, or spend an additional four to five days to trek to base camp from the nearest town, Sugapa.[https://summits.com/peaks/indonesia-puncak-jaya/112#:~:text=A%3APuncak%20Jaya%20(Carstensz%20Pyramid,jungle%20trek%20through%20dangerous%20areas.Puncak Jaya (Carstensz Pyramid): The 7th Summit is a tough climb] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241005162431/https://summits.com/peaks/indonesia-puncak-jaya-carstensz-pyramid/112#:~:text=A%3APuncak%20Jaya%20(Carstensz%20Pyramid,jungle%20trek%20through%20dangerous%20areas.Puncak|date=5 October 2024}}. Summits.com. Retrieved 28 May 2023 ===Incidents=== In 2016, Erik Airlangga died of hypothermia while attempting the peak after getting caught in extreme weather.{{Cite web |last=Dharma Somba |first=Nethy |date=April 17, 2016 |title=Freeport employee dies on Carstensz Peak - National |url=https://www.thejakartapost.com/news/2016/04/17/freeport-employee-dies-on-carstensz-peak.html |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=The Jakarta Post |language=en}} In 2017, Ahmad Hadi died of hypoxemia while climbing the peak.{{Cite web |last=Darma Somba |first=Nethy |date=October 10, 2017 |title=Dead climber airlifted from Carstensz Pyramid - National |url=https://www.thejakartapost.com/news/2017/10/10/dead-climber-airlifted-from-carstensz-pyramid.html |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=The Jakarta Post |language=en}} In the 2024 climbing season, two climbers died while attempting the summit. The first died of a suspected heart attack on 29 September. The second climber, Chinese mountaineer Dong Fei died of a fall while on the descent.{{Cite web |last=Benavides |first=Angela |date=2024-10-25 |title=A Climber's Death Mars the Long-Awaited Opening of Carstensz Pyramid » Explorersweb |url=https://explorersweb.com/a-climbers-death-mars-the-long-awaited-opening-of-carstensz-pyramid/ |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=Explorersweb}} In 2025, Lilie Wijayati Poegiono and Elsa Laksono died of hypothermia while descending the summit after being trapped in extreme weather.{{Cite web |last=Sephiawardhani |first=Diffa |date=3 March 2025 {{Short description|Highest mountain in New Zealand}} {{Redirect2|Aoraki|Mount Cook||Aoraki (disambiguation)|and|Mount Cook (disambiguation)}} {{For|the town|Mount Cook Village}} {{For|the national park|Aoraki / Mount Cook National Park}} {{Use New Zealand English|date=January 2017}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2022}} {{Infobox mountain | name = Aoraki / Mount Cook | image = File:Mt Cook LC0247.jpg | image_caption = Aoraki / Mount Cook seen from [[Hooker Valley Track|Hooker Valley]] | elevation_m = 3724 | prominence_m = 3724 | prominence_ref =
[[List of peaks by prominence|Ranked 39th]] | range = [[Southern Alps]] | listing = [[List of countries by highest point|Country high point]]
[[Ultra prominent peak|Ultra]]
[[Topographic isolation#Isolation table|World's most isolated peaks]] 10th | location = [[South Island]], New Zealand | pushpin_map = New Zealand | map_caption = Location in New Zealand | pushpin_label_position = bottom | coordinates = {{coord|43|35|42|S|170|8|31|E|type:mountain_region:NZ|display=inline,title}} | coordinates_ref = {{cite web|title=Aoraki / Mount Cook, Canterbury – NZ Topo Map|url=http://www.topomap.co.nz/NZTopoMap/nz26258/Aoraki%2fMount-Cook/Canterbury|website=NZ Topo Map|publisher=[[Land Information New Zealand]]|access-date=9 September 2016}} | topo = | first_ascent = 1894 by Tom Fyfe, George Graham, Jack Clarke | easiest_route = Linda Glacier | fetchwikidata=ALL }} '''Aoraki / Mount Cook'''{{Efn|{{ipa|en|maʊnt kʊk}}; {{ipa|mi|aɔraki}}}}{{Efn|The official name, as set by the [[Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act 1998]] is ''Aoraki/Mount Cook''. Both names, ''Aoraki'' and ''Mount Cook'' are commonly used, and the mountain is also called ''Aoraki Mount Cook'', with punctuation between the names varying or omitted entirely in non-official use.|name=names}} is the highest mountain in [[New Zealand]]. Its height, {{As of|2014|lc=y}}, is listed as {{convert|3724|m|ft|abbr=off}}.{{cite news|url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/9616590/Aoraki-Mt-Cook-shrinks-by-30m|title=Aoraki/Mt Cook shrinks by 30m|work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=16 January 2014}} It is situated in the [[Southern Alps]], the mountain range that runs the length of the [[South Island]]. A popular tourist destination,{{cite web |url=http://www.doc.govt.nz/upload/documents/about-doc/role/policies-and-plans/aoraki-mount-cook-np-management-plan-1.pdf |title=Aoraki / Mount Cook National Park Management Plan 2004 |access-date=9 May 2007 |publisher=Department of Conservation | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20070614120701/http://www.doc.govt.nz/upload/documents/about-doc/role/policies-and-plans/aoraki-mount-cook-np-management-plan-1.pdf| archive-date= 14 June 2007 | url-status= live}} it is also a favourite challenge for [[mountaineer]]s. Aoraki / Mount Cook consists of three summits: from south to north, the Low Peak ({{convert|3593|m|ft|abbr=on|disp=or}}), the Middle Peak ({{convert|3717|m|ft|abbr=on|disp=or}}) and the High Peak. The summits lie slightly south and east of the main divide of the Southern Alps, with the [[Tasman Glacier]] to the east and the [[Hooker Glacier (New Zealand)|Hooker Glacier]] to the southwest. Mount Cook is ranked 10th in the world by [[topographic isolation]].{{cite journal |last1=Kirmse |first1=Andrew |last2=de Ferranti |first2=Jonathan |title=Calculating the prominence and isolation of every mountain in the world |journal=Progress in Physical Geography: Earth and Environment |date=December 2017 |volume=41 |issue=6 |pages=788–802 |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0309133317738163 |doi=10.1177/0309133317738163 |bibcode=2017PrPG...41..788K |access-date=8 May 2024|url-access=subscription }} == Location == The mountain is in the [[Aoraki / Mount Cook National Park]], in the [[Canterbury Region]]. The park was established in 1953 and along with [[Westland Tai Poutini National Park]], [[Mount Aspiring National Park]] and [[Fiordland National Park]] forms one of the [[United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization|UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]]s. The park contains more than 140 peaks standing over {{convert|2000|m|ft}} and 72 named [[glacier]]s, which cover 40 percent of its {{convert|700|km2|acre}}. The peak is located at the northern end of the [[Mount Cook Range]], where it meets with the main spine of the Main Divide, forming a massif between the Hooker Valley to the southwest and the Tasman Valley east of the mountain. These two valleys provide the closest easily accessible view points of Aoraki / Mount Cook. A lookout point at the end of the [[Hooker Valley Track]] located only {{convert|10|km|mi|sigfig=1}} from the peak has views of the entire mountainside.{{cite web|title=Hooker Valley Track|url=http://www.newzealand.com/int/feature/hooker-valley-track/|publisher=[[Tourism New Zealand]]|access-date=30 August 2016}}{{cite web archived|title=Alpine Highs in Aoraki/Mt.Cook|url=http://www.newstalkzb.co.nz/lifestyle/travel/mike-yardley-alpine-highs-in-aorakimtcook/|publisher=[[Newstalk ZB]]|author=Mike Yardley|date=26 August 2016|access-date=31 August 2016|archive-date=19 November 2018|url-status=dead}} The settlement of [[Mount Cook Village]], also referred to as "Aoraki / Mount Cook", is a tourist centre and base camp for the mountain. It is {{nowrap|{{convert|7|km}}}} from the end of the Tasman Glacier and {{convert|15|km}} south of Aoraki / Mount Cook's summit.{{cite web|title=Aoraki / Mount Cook, Canterbury – NZ Topo Map|url=http://www.topomap.co.nz/NZTopoMap/nz26116/Aoraki%2fMount-Cook/Canterbury|website=NZ Topo Map|publisher=[[Land Information New Zealand]]|access-date=25 August 2016}} On clear days, Aoraki / Mount Cook is visible from the West Coast as far north as [[Perpendicular Point|Te Miko]], some {{cvt|194|km|mi|-1}} away,{{Cite web |title=TheViewShed - Elevate Your Perspective |url=https://theviewshed.com/?view=12035 |access-date=2026-08-13 |website=TheViewShed |language=en}} and from most of State Highway 80 along [[Lake Pukaki]] and State Highway 6 south of Lake Pukaki. The near horizontal ridge connecting the mountain's three summits forms a distinctive blocky shape when viewed from an eastern or western direction. Another popular view point is from [[Lake Matheson]] on the West Coast, described as the "view of views", where on calm days, the peaks of Aoraki / Mount Cook and Mt Tasman are reflected in Lake Matheson.{{cite web|url=http://www.doc.govt.nz/parks-and-recreation/places-to-go/west-coast/places/westland-tai-poutini-national-park/things-to-do/tracks/lake-matheson-walk/|title=Lake Matheson Walk|publisher=Department of Conservation|access-date=9 September 2016}} ==Local climate== Aoraki / Mount Cook receives substantial [[Orography|orographic precipitation]] throughout the year, as breezy, moisture-laden westerly winds dominate all year-round, bringing rainclouds from the [[Tasman Sea]] with them. [[File:Aoraki Mount Cook view from helicopter with Franz Joseph Glacier below.jpg|thumb|Aoraki / Mount Cook from above [[Franz Joseph Glacier]]]] Annual precipitation around the mountain ranges varies greatly as the local climate is dominated by the eastward movement of depressions and anticyclones from across the Tasman Sea. The Aoraki / Mount Cook massif is a major obstacle to the prevailing westerly winds as they push depressions and associated cold fronts of moist air from the subtropics in the northwest against the mountain range. As the air rises towards the peaks, it expands and cools, and forms clouds. Rain and snowfall are often heaviest around the {{convert|1200|m|abbr=on}} level and can last for several days if the front is slow-moving.{{cite web|url=http://www.doc.govt.nz/documents/getting-involved/students-and-teachers/field-trips-by-region/canterbury/aoraki/aoraki-mt-cook-education-resource-colour.pdf|title=Aoraki / Mount Cook Education Resource|year=2010|publisher=Department of Conservation|page=16|access-date=13 September 2016}} As a result of the local weather patterns, the western slopes of Aoraki / Mount Cook can receive well over {{convert|10000|mm|in|abbr=on|sigfig=1}} of annual precipitation, whereas the nearby Mount Cook Village, only {{convert|15|km|0|abbr=on}} south of the mountain, receives {{convert|4484|mm|in|1|abbr=on}} of rain or snowfall.{{cite web | url = http://www.niwa.co.nz/education-and-training/schools/resources/climate | title = Climate Data and Activities | date = 28 February 2007 | publisher = NIWA Science | access-date = 15 October 2013}} While the weather on the eastern side of the mountain is generally better, rain or snow can quickly become widespread on that side as well if the wind turns to the south or southeast. This brings with it a rapid drop in temperature and poor visibility, adding to the difficult climbing conditions on Aoraki / Mount Cook.{{cite news|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11381328|title=Climbers missing on Aoraki-Mt Cook may never be found|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|date=3 January 2015|access-date=13 September 2016}} Temperatures at the mountain's base in the Hooker Valley around {{convert|800|m|abbr=off}} range from {{convert|-13|C|abbr=on}} to {{convert|32|C|abbr=on}}, and generally fall just over {{cvt|1|C-change}} for every {{convert|200|m}} of altitude.{{cite web|url=http://www.doc.govt.nz/documents/getting-involved/students-and-teachers/field-trips-by-region/canterbury/aoraki/aoraki-mt-cook-education-resource-colour.pdf|title=Aoraki / Mount Cook Education Resource|year=2010|publisher=Department of Conservation|page=8|access-date=13 September 2016}} From about {{convert|1000|m|abbr=on|sigfig=1}} and higher, semi-permanent snow and ice fields exist during winter. Winter and spring are usually less settled than summer and autumn. Anticyclones often bring days of settled weather in summer, or clear cold conditions in winter with severe frost.{{cite web|url=https://www.niwa.co.nz/education-and-training/schools/resources/climate/overview/map_alpine|title=Map Alpine|date=28 February 2007|publisher=[[National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research|NIWA]]|access-date=13 September 2016}} ==Naming and European discovery== [[File:Mtcook1600x1200.jpg|thumb|left|Aoraki / Mount Cook seen from the south, taken from {{convert|4000|m|ft|0}}]] In the traditions of the [[Ngāi Tahu]] iwi an early name for the South Island is ''{{lang|mi|Te Waka o Aoraki}}'' ('Aoraki's Canoe'). In the past many believed it meant "Cloud Piercer",{{cite web |url=http://www.teara.govt.nz/NewZealanders/MaoriNewZealanders/NgaiTahu/2/ENZ-Resources/Standard/1/en |title=Ngāi Tahu – Aoraki – Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand |access-date=8 May 2007 |author=Te Maire Tau |date=21 December 2006 |publisher=Ministry for Culture and Heritage / Te Manatū Taonga }} a romantic rendering of the name's components: ''{{lang|mi|ao}}'' (world, daytime, cloud, etc.) and ''{{lang|mi|raki}}'' or ''{{lang|mi|rangi}}'' (day, sky, weather, etc.).{{cite web|url=http://www.maoridictionary.co.nz/ |title=Māori Dictionary Online |publisher=Maoridictionary.co.nz |access-date=22 July 2016}} Historically, the [[Māori language|Māori]] name has been spelt ''{{lang|mi|Aorangi}}'', using the northern dialect. Aoraki / Mount Cook became known to Māori after their arrival in New Zealand some time around the 14th century CE. The first Europeans who may have seen Aoraki / Mount Cook were members of [[Abel Tasman]]'s crew, who saw a "large land uplifted high" (probably some part of the Southern Alps) while off the west coast of the South Island, just north of present-day Greymouth{{cite web |url=http://www.teara.govt.nz/NewZealanders/NewZealandPeoples/EuropeanDiscoveryOfNewZealand/2/en/ |title=European discovery of New Zealand – Abel Tasman – Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand |access-date=8 May 2007 |author=John Wilson |date=21 December 2006 |publisher=Ministry for Culture and Heritage / Te Manatū Taonga }}{{cite encyclopedia|url=http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/european-discovery-of-new-zealand/page-2 |title=European discovery of New Zealand – Abel Tasman |encyclopedia=Te Ara – The Encyclopedia of New Zealand |date=9 December 2015 |access-date=22 July 2016}} on 13 December 1642 during Tasman's first Pacific voyage. The English name of ''Mount Cook'' was given to the mountain in 1851 by Captain [[John Lort Stokes]] to honour Captain [[James Cook]] who surveyed and circumnavigated the islands of New Zealand in 1770. Captain Cook did not sight the mountain during his exploration.{{cite book|url=https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/8106 |title=Captain Cook's Journal During the First Voyage Round the World |access-date=9 May 2007 |author=James Cook |date=1728–1779 |pages=Sunday, 18 March 1770 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070416114512/http://www.gutenberg.org/etext/8106 |archive-date=16 April 2007 |url-status=live }} Following the [[treaty of Waitangi claims and settlements|settlement]] between Ngāi Tahu and the Crown in 1998, a number of South Island place names were amended to incorporate their Māori names by the [[Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act 1998]]. The name of the mountain was officially changed from Mount Cook to Aoraki/Mount Cook to incorporate its historic Māori name.{{cite web |url=http://www.beehive.govt.nz/feature/ngai-tahu-settlement-260 |title=Ngāi Tahu Settlement Section 3: Aoraki / Mount Cook |first=Doug |last=Graham |publisher=New Zealand Government |date=13 October 1998 |access-date=10 June 2012 }} It is the only one of these names where the Māori name precedes the English. Under the settlement the Crown agreed to return title of Aoraki / Mount Cook to Ngāi Tahu, who would then formally gift it back to the nation. Neither transfer has yet occurred, and Ngāi Tahu can decide when this will happen.{{cite news |first=Claire |last=Trevett |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=10645708 |title=Tuhoe veto followed parks advice |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=18 May 2010 }} ==Geology== [[File:mtcook.nz.750pix.jpg|thumb|Aoraki / Mount Cook from Landsat 7]] The Southern Alps in the South Island were formed by [[tectonics|tectonic]] uplifting and pressure as the [[Pacific Plate|Pacific]] and [[Indo-Australian Plate]]s collided along the island's western coast. The uplifting continues, raising Aoraki / Mount Cook an average of {{convert|7|mm|in}} each year. However, erosive forces are also powerful shapers of the mountains. The severe weather is due to the mountain's jutting into powerful westerly winds of the [[Roaring Forties]] which run around approximately 45°S latitude, south of both Africa and Australia. The Southern Alps are the first obstacle the winds encounter after South America, having moved east across the [[Southern Ocean]]. The height of Aoraki / Mount Cook was established in 1881 by G. J. Roberts (from the west side) and in 1889 by T. N. Brodrick (from the Canterbury side). Their measurements agreed closely at {{convert|12349|ft|m}}. The height was reduced by {{convert|10|m|ft}} when approximately 12–14 million cubic metres of rock and ice fell off the northern peak on 14 December 1991.The landslide carried with it another 40 million cubic metres of rock and ice. The impact caused an earth quake of 3.9 on the Richter scale. [P207 In search Of Ancient NZ.Campball and Hutching.GNS science/Penguin.2011.] {{cite web |url=http://www.teara.govt.nz/EarthSeaAndSky/NaturalHazardsAndDisasters/Landslides/2/ENZ-Resources/Standard/1/en |title=Mt Cook landslide |access-date=3 May 2007 |author=Michael J. Crozier |publisher=Te Ara — the Encyclopedia of New Zealand }}{{cite web archived|url=http://tpo.tepapa.govt.nz/ViewTopicExhibitDetail.asp?ExhibitionID=0x000a4de2&ExhibitID=0x000a4ede&Language=English |title=Mount Aoraki (Mount Cook) rock avalanche |access-date=3 May 2007 |author=T. J. Chinn |author2=M. J. McSaveney |date=1992 |publisher=Tai Awatea — Knowledge Net (More of Te Papa online) |url-status=dead |archive-date=27 September 2007 }} Two decades of erosion of the ice cap exposed after this collapse reduced the height by another {{cvt|30|m|ft}} to {{cvt|3724|m|ft}}.{{cite news |title=Height of NZ's tallest peak Aoraki/Mt Cook slashed by 30m |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11187423 |access-date=16 January 2014 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=16 January 2014 }}{{cite web |url=http://www.otago.ac.nz/news/news/otago062651.html |title=Otago-led study revises height of Aoraki/Mt Cook |publisher=[[University of Otago]] |access-date=22 July 2016}} Aoraki / Mount Cook lies in the centre of the distinctive [[Alpine Fault]], a {{cvt|650|km|mi}} long [[active fault]] in the Southern Alps. It is responsible for the uplift of Aoraki / Mount Cook and is believed to move every 100 to 300 years. It last moved in 1717.Campball and Hutching. ''In Search of Ancient New Zealand'', p. 139. ==Surrounding forests and glaciers== [[File:Aoraki (Mount Cook) from Hooker Glacier Lake.jpg|thumb|right|upright=1.7|Aoraki / Mount Cook as seen from the end of the [[Hooker Valley Track]], with the Hooker Glacier's [[moraine-dammed lake|moraine lake]] in the foreground.]] The average annual rainfall in the surrounding lowlands, in particular to the west, is around {{convert|5|to|10|m|in}}. This very high rainfall leads to temperate [[rainforest]]s in these coastal lowlands and a reliable source of snow in the mountains to keep the glaciers flowing. These include the [[Tasman Glacier]] to the east of the mountain and the smaller [[Hooker Glacier (New Zealand)|Hooker Glacier]] immediately to its south. The vegetation in the valleys to the east, in particular the Tasman Valley, is noticeably less lush than that on the western slopes of the mountain. Forest would normally grow to about {{cvt|1300|m|ft}} in this area, but a lack of soil due to scree, rock falls and the effects of glaciation prevent this in most localities around the mountain. [[Tussock grasslands of New Zealand|Snow tussock]] and other alpine plants cling to as high as {{cvt|1900|m|ft}}. Above the snowline, only [[lichen]] can be found amongst the rock, snowfields and ice that dominate the highest parts of Aoraki / Mount Cook.{{cite web|url=http://www.doc.govt.nz/documents/getting-involved/students-and-teachers/field-trips-by-region/canterbury/aoraki/aoraki-mt-cook-education-resource-colour.pdf|title=Aoraki / Mount Cook Education Resource|year=2010|publisher=Department of Conservation|page=17|access-date=7 September 2016}} ==Climbing history== [[File:MountCook-P1140884a.jpg|thumb|left|View of Aoraki / Mount Cook from the Tasman Lake south of the mountain]] The first recorded attempt on the summit was made by the Irishman Rev. [[William S. Green]], the Swiss hotelier Emil Boss, and the Swiss mountain guide [[Ulrich Kaufmann]] on 2 March 1882 via the Tasman and Linda Glaciers. {{cite book | last = Green | first = Reverend William Spotswood | title = The High Alps of New Zealand, or A Trip to the Glaciers of The Antipodes with an Ascent of Mount Cook | date = 1883 }} They came within a few feet of the top, as did the 1890 ascent attempt by Mannering and Dixon.{{cite journal |last1=Harper |first1=A. P. |title=Exploration and Character of the Principal New Zealand Glaciers |journal=The Geographical Journal |date=Jan 1893 |volume=1 |issue=1 |page=38}} [[File:On Mt. Cook, New Zealand. 1977.jpg|thumb|On Aoraki / Mount Cook, 1977]] The first known ascent was on 25 December 1894, when New Zealanders [[Tom Fyfe]], John Michael (Jack) Clarke and George Graham reached the summit via the Hooker Valley and the north ridge.Haynes, J. (1994) ''Piercing the Clouds. Tom Fyffe: First to climb Mt Cook''. Hazard Press, New Zealand, {{ISBN|0-908790-64-3}}. Despite an earlier failed attempt on 20 December, the local climbers were spurred on by their desire for the first ascent to be made by New Zealand mountaineers amid reports that the American mountaineer [[Edward FitzGerald (mountaineer)|Edward FitzGerald]] had his eye on the summit.{{cite encyclopedia|title=Aoraki/Mt Cook|url=http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/mountaineering/3#2|encyclopedia=[[Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand]] |access-date=28 March 2010}} The party reached the summit at approximately 1:30 pm after bounding up the last leg of the mountain full of excitement at reaching the top.{{cite encyclopedia|title=Mountaineering – First Ascent Aoraki/Mt Cook|url=http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/mountaineering/3/4|encyclopedia=[[Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand]] |access-date=28 March 2011}} The route they had successfully traversed was not repeated again until the 100th ascent over 60 years later in 1955. Swiss guide [[Matthias Zurbriggen]] of FitzGerald's party made the second ascent on 14 March 1895 from the Tasman Glacier side, via the ridge that now bears his name. This is credited as the first solo ascent, although Zurbriggen was accompanied part of the way up the ridge by J Adamson.{{cite journal | title = Mountaineering in the Southern Alps of New Zealand | journal =Alpine Journal| date= 1895| first =E.A. | last = Fitzgerald | issn= 0065-6569 |volume =#17 | pages=469–475 | access-date =20 December 2025 |url = https://alpinejournal.org.uk/Contents/Contents_1895_files/AJ%201895%20Vol%2017%20469-475%20Fitzgerald%20New%20Zealand.pdf }} After Zurbriggen's ascent it was another ten years before the mountain was climbed again. In February 1905 Jack Clarke with four others completed the third ascent following Zurbriggen's route. Clarke therefore became the first person to do a repeat ascent.{{Cite web |title=Profile {{!}} South Canterbury Museum |url=https://museum.timaru.govt.nz/explore/scroll/profile?id=1216 |access-date=2023-10-15 |website=museum.timaru.govt.nz}} The first woman to ascend the mountain was Australian [[Freda Du Faur]] on 3 December 1910. Local guide George Bannister, a nephew of another guide, [[Butler Te Koeti]] of Ngāi Tahu,[http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/3t15/te-koeti-turanga-pahikore " Te Koeti Turanga"], te Ara was the first [[Māori people|Māori]] to successfully scale the peak in 1912.{{cite encyclopedia|url=http://www.teara.govt.nz/TheBush/BushAndMountainRecreation/Mountaineering/4/en |title=Mountaineering – Guided climbing |encyclopedia=Te Ara – The Encyclopedia of New Zealand |date=15 October 2014 |access-date=22 July 2016}} A traverse of the three peaks was first accomplished in 1913 by Freda Du Faur and guides [[Alec and Peter Graham]]. This 'grand traverse' was repeated in January 1916 by [[Conrad Kain]], guiding the 57-year-old [[Jane Thomson (mountaineer)|Jane Thomson]], considered at the time "a marvellous feat unequalled for daring in the annals of the Southern Alps".{{cite journal|last=Thorington|first=J. Monroe (J.M.T.)|url=http://publications.americanalpineclub.org/articles/12193423600/Conrad-Kain-1833-1934|title=Conrad Kain, 1833–1934 – In Memoriam"|journal=American Alpine Journal|volume=2|page=236|year=1934}} [[Edmund Hillary|Sir Edmund Hillary]] made his first ascent in January 1948. In February 1948 with Ruth Adams, Harry Ayres and Mick Sullivan, Hillary made the first ascent of the South Ridge to the Low Peak.{{cite book|first=Sir Edmund|last=Hillary|author-link=Edmund Hillary|title=View from the Summit|page=62|publisher=Pocket Books|location=New York|year=1999|isbn=0-7434-0067-4}} To celebrate the life of Hillary the South Ridge was renamed as Hillary Ridge in August 2011.{{cite web|url=http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/national/82214/south-ridge-of-mt-cook-to-be-renamed-hillary-ridge|title=South Ridge of Mt Cook to be renamed Hillary Ridge|date=11 August 2011|publisher=[[Radio New Zealand]] |access-date=10 August 2011}} Aoraki / Mount Cook is a technically challenging mountain with a high level of glaciation. Its level of difficulty is often underestimated and can change dramatically depending on weather, snow and ice conditions. The climb crosses large crevasses, and involves risks of ice and rock falls, avalanches and rapidly changing weather conditions. Since the early 20th century, around 80 people have died attempting to climb the mountain,{{cite news|url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/64350575/Mt-Cook-Does-reaching-summit-outweigh-risks|title=Mt Cook: Does reaching summit outweigh risks?|work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]]|author=Anna Pearson|date=20 December 2014|access-date=9 September 2016}} making it New Zealand's deadliest peak. The climbing season traditionally runs from November to February, and hardly a season goes by without at least one fatality. ==Māori history, legends and traditions== [[File:Hooker Valley towards Aoraki Mount Cook at sunset.jpg|thumb|Aoraki / Mount Cook at sunset from Hooker Valley]] According to [[Māori culture|Māori]] legend, Aoraki was a young boy who, along with his three brothers, were the sons of [[Rangi and Papa|Rakinui]], the Sky Father. On their voyage around the [[Rangi and Papa|Papatūānuku]], the Earth Mother, their canoe became stranded on a reef and tilted. Aoraki and his brothers climbed onto the top side of their canoe. However, the south wind froze them and turned them to stone. Their canoe became the Te Waka o Aoraki, the [[South Island]], and their prows, the [[Marlborough Sounds]]. Aoraki, the tallest, became the highest peak, and his brothers created the Kā Tiritiri o te Moana, the [[Southern Alps]]. {{cite web |url=http://www.tourism.net.nz/new-zealand/about-new-zealand/regions/mt-cook-and-mackenzie-country/history.html|title=Aoraki/Mt Cook – History |publisher=New Zealand Tourism Guide |access-date=13 July 2010}} {{cite encyclopedia |url=http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/ngai-tahu/2/1 |title=Aoraki (Mt Cook) in the Southern Alps |encyclopedia=Te Ara – The Encyclopedia of New Zealand |access-date=13 July 2010}} {{cite web |url=http://www.doc.govt.nz/upload/documents/getting-involved/students-and-teachers/field-trips-by-region/canterbury/aoraki/aoraki-mt-cook-education-resource-colour.pdf|title=Aoraki / Mount Cook Education Resource |date=2010 |publisher=Department of Conservation |page=5 |access-date=14 July 2010}} Ngāi Tahu, the main iwi (tribe) of New Zealand's southern region, consider Aoraki as the most sacred of the ancestors that they had descended from. Aoraki brings the iwi with its sense of community and purpose, and remains the physical form of Aoraki and the link between the worlds of the supernatural and nature. ==Post-contact timeline== * 1642 – Aoraki was possibly sighted by [[Abel Tasman]] and crew members.{{cite encyclopedia|url=http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/european-discovery-of-new-zealand/page-2|title=2. – European discovery of New Zealand – Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand |encyclopedia=[[Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand]] |date=11 May 2016|access-date=7 September 2016}} * 1770 – Captain Cook named Kā-Tiritiri-o-te-moana "the Southern Alps". * 1851 – Captain [[John Lort Stokes]] of the survey ship [[HMS Acheron (1838)|HMS ''Acheron'']] gave the name Mount Cook to Aoraki. * 1894 – The first known ascent of Aoraki took place on 25 December, by [[Jack Clarke (mountaineer)|Jack Clarke]], [[Tom Fyfe]] and [[George Graham (mountaineer)|George Graham]]. * 1910 – [[Freda du Faur]] became the first known woman to climb Aoraki. * 1913 – The first ascents of The Footstool and Kakīroa (or Maukatua, Mount Sefton) were made by Freda du Faur's climbing party. * 1914 – The first recorded fatal accident occurred, when three men were caught in avalanche on Linda Glacier. * 1975 – Four [[Royal New Zealand Air Force]] personnel were killed during a mountain survival training exercise near the Ball Pass, when they were buried alive by an avalanche. * 1982 – [[Mark Inglis]] and his climbing partner Phillip Doole were trapped in a [[snow cave]] for 13 days in an intense blizzard. During his rescue an RNZAF 3 Squadron [[Bell UH-1H]] [[No. 3 Squadron RNZAF#Accidents|crashed]] on Aoraki. * 1982 – Geoff Wyatt and John Blennehasset achieved the first ski descent from the summit. * 1991 – An avalanche of 10 million cubic metres of snow and rock caused {{convert|10|m|ft}} to be lost off the top of Aoraki. Two decades of erosion of the ice cap exposed after this collapse reduced the height by another {{cvt|30|m|ft}} to {{cvt|3724|m|ft}}, as revealed by new GPS data from a University of Otago climbing expedition in November 2013.{{cite news|title=Height of NZ's tallest peak Aoraki/Mt Cook slashed by 30m|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11187423|access-date=6 September 2016|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|date=16 January 2014}}{{cite web| url = http://www.otago.ac.nz/news/news/otago062651.html| title = Otago-led study revises height of Aoraki/Mt Cook|publisher=University of Otago|date=16 January 2014|access-date=2023-05-28}} * 1998 – The [[Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act 1998|Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act]] officially recognised the original name, renaming the mountain Aoraki / Mount Cook. == Other == In 2027, Aoraki / Mount Cook will become one of four natural attractions that will start charging entry fees for foreign tourists.
